Furthermore, as the house will recall, an additional sum of a like amount was made available in the amendments to the National Housing Act which the house adopted in December. Not only has the first $150 million been fully taken up but already, notwithstanding the fact that we are in the winter months, no less than $35 million of that additional $150 million has already been taken up.
I think, Mr. Speaker, it must be quite evident to all hon. members that the government has done much to assist the house contraction industry and bring great benefits to Canadians in the housing field.

subtopic: ADMISSION OF CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT AND WORKMEN FROM UNITED STATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ADMISSION OF CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT AND WORKMEN FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a two-pronged question. The shorter prong is directed to the
Inquiries of the Ministry Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and the longer prong is directed to the Minister of National Revenue in the hope of skewering him.
In view of the fact that the owners of idle construction equipment in British Columbia are complaining that United States mining companies are permitted to bring their equipment of various kinds into Canada together with the employees necessary to do this type of work, while Canadian equipment and employees remain idle, would the minister inquire into this situation and take action to safeguard the interests of unemployed Canadian citizens?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: ADMISSION OF CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT AND WORKMEN FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it shows the sporting instinct of the hon. gentleman that he should direct the longer prong toward the longer person. I, of course, have nothing to say with respect to the entry of United States workmen into Canada. That is a matter for another department. In so far as the reference to machinery is concerned, it is true that under our tariff act certain types of mining machinery are allowed entry into Canada free of duty, under the old principle that they are used for the development of Canadian natural resources. That, of course, is a matter of legislation.
The question confuses mining with construction, and I am not quite sure whether its terms cover construction machinery or mining machinery. If it is mining machinery then, as I have said, certain types enter free of duty. In so far as construction machinery is concerned, that does not enter free of duty and since my term of office began, at least, there have been no special concessions made to permit the entry of any construction machinery from the United States into Canada except on payment of the regular tariffs. A surplus of secondhand machinery overhangs the American market at the moment, and my officials are watchful to see that this machinery is very carefully appraised for customs duty before admission to Canada.

subtopic: ADMISSION OF CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT AND WORKMEN FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: It is mining machinery that can be used on construction in Canada. I thank the minister for his explanation and I will let him know the facts later. If you could stop the machinery you would stop the men, because the men are brought in because they are necessary to work the machines.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMISSION OF CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT AND WORKMEN FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with reference to the second and shorter prong of the question, I know the hon. gentleman's

Inquiries of the Ministry concern, and I have on occasions expressed similar concern with regard to the general situation.
But I must say that the officials of the department are aware of the importance of not letting into Canada those who will take employment that should otherwise be available to Canadians, and are watchful to see that this is not done.
I cannot, of course, assert positively that there has not been any case in which someone has slipped past them. I can only say that in order to be certain of the situation it is essential that we should have any specific complaint drawn to our attention by name and location in order that we may deal with it. Without such information it is impossible to do anything more than give the general assurance that I now give.

subtopic: ADMISSION OF CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT AND WORKMEN FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: I will get that information from the persons who complained.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA-INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT STATUS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think there is some truth in the story although not exactly in the form of the words used. I think the fact that Mr. Hanna came to the immigration department office in Vancouver and asked for help indicates a rather greater degree of confidence and friendship between him and the department under the new conditions than existed under the former administration. It is true that Mr. Hanna did come to the department in Vancouver and asked for help, and we are now looking into the question to see what help we can give him.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA-INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT STATUS
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman say whether Mr. Hanna is employed at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: C. G. HANNA-INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT STATUS
speechtext: I am not able to answer that question as of today, Mr. Speaker. He came to us and asked help in obtaining employment at sea.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA-INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT STATUS
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman aware that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard guaranteed this gentleman employment, and guaranteed it to his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

subtopic: ILES-DE-LA-MADELEINE    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR REPAIR OF WHARF AT GRINDSTONE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ILES-DE-LA-MADELEINE    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR REPAIR OF WHARF AT GRINDSTONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine asked me this question, as reported at page 3291 of Hansard:
On January 7 last I drew the attention of the minister to damage to the wharf at Grindstone and the urgency of making repairs. I suggested that steel for the repairs should be ordered immediately. My question is, have instructions been given in his department for the steel to be ordered?
The answer to this question is that following the storm damage certain emergency repairs were undertaken to prevent further damage to the structure. These repairs are only temporary, and the reconstruction of the damaged area is being studied at the present time. It is not expected that this reconstruction can be completed before the opening of the navigation season.
Atlantic Provinces Power Development POWER

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 244, to provide assistance in respect of electric power development in the Atlantic provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think any hon. member will be surprised to find that I am taking the rather unusual course of speaking once more on this measure on third reading.
You have a full gallery today.

That, I may say, is the kind of remark I would expect from the source from which it came.
I am speaking, sir, because I feel there is still time to appeal to the government to change their minds about the refusal they have made up to now to make this bill in any effective way applicable to one of the four Atlantic provinces. I was not able to be here yesterday at the committee stage because of the discourtesy of the government in refusing to hold this measure over in spite of the assurance we were given by the Prime Minister on Monday when we accepted the motion.

The hon.
member is entitled to talk about discourtesy as well as anybody in this house.
Well, I shall not endeavour to compete in the realm of discourtesy with the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, who is a past master.

You are
competing with your friends in the Coliseum right now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would ask hon. members to allow the member who has the floor to continue, and I would hope that he will not follow the trend he has been following.

Mr. Speaker, it is evident that there are quite a few members on the back benches of the opposite side of the house who were not in the last parliament, and therefore they would not know that the very mild and courteous remarks that are made from this side of the house now represent no discourtesy.
Oh, oh.

They should have heard the Minister of Finance when he was over here. They should have heard the Minister of Public Works persisting when he was over here.

Atlantic Provinces Power Development

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member has forgotten the title of the bill.

I think perhaps, sir, it is the government that has forgotten the title of the bill. I thank Your Honour for drawing it to my attention so that I may draw it once more to the attention of the government. The purpose of the bill purportedly-and I borrow the word of the hon. member for St. John's West, the Minister without Portfolio-is to assist the four Atlantic provinces, but the government have been most careful to make sure that it will give no effective assistance to one of these four provinces.
That is why I am rising at this stage of the measure to protest the conduct of the government, to protest the fact that they did not accede to the request made by the premier of Newfoundland to have a very small amendment made in the bill which would have made it possible for the government to help the province of Newfoundland, and to ask if they would not consider postponing third reading and referring the bill back to committee in order to make that amendment even at this late stage.
Although I believe it might be in order, it seems to me that it would be useless for me to move an amendment to that effect. I think probably I will be more likely to succeed in my appeal if I attempt to show how completely this measure will fail to be of any effective assistance to Newfoundland, and appeal to the government to make this one change which would commit them to no specific project but would enable them to consider specific projects and not have to come back to parliament for authority to carry them out.
That is the very modest request that was made by the premier of Newfoundland to the Prime Minister, about which the Prime Minister apparently did not think it worth while to inform his colleague, the Minister without Portfolio, and which we were told the other day had never been discussed in the cabinet.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I do not know where the hon. member gets that statement. He has made it several times before. I did not say the matter was not discussed in the cabinet and I could not say anything about what was discussed in the cabinet. The hon. member, a member of a former government, knows I could not say anything about what was discussed in cabinet, so I wish he would not make references of that kind.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has made his point, but it is really not a question of privilege. It is a correction of a statement. May I remind members of the house that the

proper procedure is to allow the member who has the floor to finish his speech and then rise to make corrections.

I thank Your Honour, and I may say in explanation and in fairness to the hon. member that I think he has a point. He did not say this matter had never been considered in the cabinet. He did not say he had not received a copy of the telegram from the Prime Minister. I inferred both these things, and I inferred them from the statement he did make in the house, which is on Hansard and which the hon. gentleman remembers well, that the only way he heard about this matter was through receiving from Newfoundland what purported to be a copy of a telegram from the premier of Newfoundland. If that does not suggest to any unprejudiced mind that my conclusion is correct I do not know what would.
I do not think there is any useful purpose in pursuing that matter any further. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, when I was unable to be in the house
yesterday-
Why?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You know why.
He was fighting with Paul Martin.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You were not decent enough to adjourn for the convention. You know why.

I was not able to be here for good and sufficient reasons having to do with the choice of the person who will be the second most important officer of this house. It does seem to me that is just as adequate as the excuses that used to be accepted by Mr. Walter Harris when he led the house for postponing business to oblige hon. members when they were on this side, a courtesy which we do not get now.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
I suppose we are going to have another phony question of privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, no one can have any objection to the hon. member dealing with the merits or demerits of this measure, but repeatedly this morning he has dragged in other things which are not material and which are merely the cheapest kind of political tub thumping.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I submit that he is out of order.
The hon. gentleman is out of order now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister has a point. There has been a departure from the subject matter of the debate on third reading. On the other hand there has been a certain amount of provocation, and I ask members on both sides of the house to try to stick to the matter under discussion.
Well, sir, as I think any unprejudiced hon. member will admit, I have always tried to do so since I came into this parliament-
Oh, oh.

-and I will endeavour, so far as I know them, to abide completely by the rules. I want first, sir, to refer to the statement made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources yesterday when he said, as found on page 3304 of Hansard:
I feel It is clear also from the Prime Minister's remarks that the aid will be for publicly owned systems.
Then he went on to suggest that these publicly owned systems might, under some arrangement made by the provinces, be associated in some way with private companies, but that there would be no direct aid to private companies. I am trying to save time by merely summarizing what he said, and if my statement is not correct I will be very glad to read his words. The point I am making is that the hon. gentleman said that under this bill no aid to a private company would be possible. Is that correct? If it is not correct, I should like to be corrected, because I want to be completely fair in this matter. I assume, therefore, it is correct.
The hon. member for St. John's West spoke on this subject on Monday, and what he said will be found at page 3262 of Hansard. I think I had better quote the hon. gentleman's words so as to leave no doubt as to the accuracy of what I am saying. He said:
Let us see what this government is going to do for Newfoundland.
Well, we would certainly like to see it. I am quoting the hon. member for St. John's West, the Minister without Portfolio.
In Newfoundland, as I stated, we have private companies which have developed power which they are anxious to sell. They can increase that power by using their own resources and without looking for any loan at all.
Now, sir, that is precisely what we are objecting to. The hon. member said the Newfoundland Light and Power Company, if that is the correct name of the company, was planning an extension of its thermal plant in St. John's, and he says now that company has plenty of resources to do it on its own and therefore does not need any help under this bill.
Atlantic Provinces Power Development
The hon. gentleman said later in his speech that it would, of course, make power cheaper in Newfoundland, or anywhere else, to get a loan at the advantageous rate of interest that was available under the Beechwood measure. It would certainly be an even greater advantage, one would have thought, to obtain assistance under this measure for that thermal plant in St. John's. But because this government will not, as we intended to do, give any assistance to private companies but insist upon power projects being publicly owned, this aid is going to be denied to the company in Newfoundland.
When did your government intend to do it?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: When the hon. member was asleep.
I have never been as asleep as you have been.

The hon. gentleman, who as we all know is one of the most alert and interested members in the house, must have been out of the house when my colleague the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet was speaking the other day and pointing out the differences between the government's measure and the very much more liberal measure we proposed last April.
I was in the house, and he did not say when they were going to do it.

It is in this respect that there is a most important difference. In spite of the fact that the Liberal government was prepared to give this assistance to privately owned companies, and was in the process of doing it-

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understood from him it was the policy of his government to give aid to privately owned companies. May I ask him why, when in March of last year the minister of fisheries, as he then was, made a statement in Vancouver that the government was prepared to extend aid to British Columbia for the development of the Columbia river, the condition was made that it must be a publicly owned development?
Well, sir-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Take another drink.

The reason was probably, and indeed was certainly, that the Liberal government at that time had made a decision which was announced in the budget, and
3344	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development which was elaborated upon by my colleague on April 9, if I remember the date correctly, to assist the Atlantic provinces in this special way. There was no plan at that time to extend this beyond the Atlantic provinces. This particular policy-

May I ask
the hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.
Will he indicate any evidence to show that the Liberal government, prior to June 10, was prepared to do anything along this line for Newfoundland?
I can say, sir, that we did not go about making any empty promises before the election, and we are not making any empty promises now.
No?
We think the Canadian people have had enough of that for a while. They will want, before very long, to get something like responsible government again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: They sure had enough of the Liberals.

In the light of the fact that the Liberal government was prepared to extend this assistance to private companies in the Atlantic provinces, as well as to publicly owned operations, and the Tory government is not, the minister had the effrontery to say that this Tory legislation confirmed the suggestions of many political observers that, in fact, during the last few years in Canada we have had a Liberal socialist government.
Here are the facts, sir. As the minister himself admitted, we were prepared to extend this aid to private companies.
What private companies?

To private power companies in the province of Nova Scotia. The Tory government refuses to do that. It does seem to me, sir, that by any definition of "socialist" or any extension of that definition I have ever heard, in what is already becoming a rather long life, it has never been suggested that a policy that supports private companies is socialist, and a policy that refuses to support them is non-socialist. Perhaps this is just another of the many evidences we have had since this parliament began this session on October 14, of the confusion and misunderstanding that exists in the minds of hon. members on the treasury benches, and to an even greater degree amongst the backbenchers on the other side.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
I should be delighted to find out if the hon. gentleman is capable of asking a question.

I am on my feet to find out if the hon. gentleman can answer one. Would the hon. gentleman please tie in his remarks with the remarks of the former fisheries minister and the former prime minister in the maritimes to the effect that maritime coal mines should be closed and the coal should be left in the ground?

To the best of my knowledge and belief no such statements were ever made by either of these gentlemen. I know absolutely and positively that no such statement was made by the former prime minister.
All this cheap Tory propaganda we have heard is based upon a speech the former prime minister made in Fredericton. I was present on the platform and heard every word of it. There was no such statement in it. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond read the relevant paragraph the other day from a shorthand report of that speech, and this report did not bear out any such nonsense as that. However, this is characteristic in my experience, and it is now becoming quite a long one, of the normal way in which Tory political campaigns are conducted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Typical Liberal wind and water.

I want to go on, sir. If hon. gentlemen opposite could just desist, and I include the Minister of Justice, from bringing in matters that are totally irrelevant to this bill and allow me to give my attention to the measure itself, I would be very happy to go on with what the hon. member for St. John's West had to say about the way in which this particular measure would be helpful to Newfoundland. I think I will put in the record a great deal of what the hon. gentleman said, because I want-
It is on now.
You cannot think of anything of your own.
Why don't you keep quiet for five minutes?
Everybody picks on "Pick".

If the hon. gentleman has any doubt about my capacity to think up a few more things to say I could relieve him of that doubt. Here is what the Minister

without Portfolio said, out of his great knowledge of power and his apparently great knowledge of Newfoundland, as reported at page 3262 of Hansard for January 13, 1958:
What we need at the moment in Newfoundland is transmission lines. The private companies hesitate to extend their lines to areas which they believe will not be profitable. These companies have already built electric power plants to supply areas in which they feel the business they are going to receive justifies the expenditure. I know that the power company operating on the southern shore, which is part of my riding of St. John's West, has during the past year extended the "lights" as we call it down there up as far as Renews.
Then the hon. gentleman went on to mention a number of other settlements farther down the shore to which power has not been extended. The hon. member for St. John's West was apparently trying to give this house, his constituents and anyone who may read Hansard the impression that the extension of distribution lines down the south shore was something that would come within the provisions of this bill. I could not believe that was correct. I was sure the hon. member was mistaken, because my recollection was that the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet, in a question to the minister sponsoring this measure, had made a clear distinction between transmission lines and distribution lines; that was in my mind.
I do not pretend to be an expert about these matters, and I try in the house not to make assertions when I am not in possession of all the facts. I therefore did not immediately challenge the observations made by the hon. member for St. John's West. But as soon as the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet came back to the house I asked him about this matter, and yesterday in committee he asked the minister about it. Here is his question and here is the minister's answer as reported at page 3305 of Hansard. Here is the question of the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet.
Order.

I am reading for the benefit of the hon. gentleman:
I have two or three questions I should like to ask the minister at this stage. Would he tell us what he understands by the term "transmission lines"? Does he distinguish between transmission lines and distribution lines? Does he understand by "transmission line" one that goes from the power plant to the distribution stations and substations or between distribution stations and distribution substations but does not include the lines going from those distribution stations or substations to the domestic or industrial users?
This is the answer given by the minister;
My understanding of "transmission line" is exactly the same as that of the hon. member for
Atlantic Provinces Power Development Montmagny-L'Islet. It goes from one plant to another or from one plant to a substation and so on and does not include distribution lines.
What the hon. member for St. John's West was talking about were distribution lines, which do not come within the scope of this bill at all. Hence his statement that this bill would enable the government to do what he said they could do for the southern shore in his own constituency is in error. I assume that the hon. gentleman made that statement out of ignorance and without any intention of misleading. I think perhaps that is the most charitable assumption it is possible to make about his statement.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that even if these transmission lines were, as the hon. gentleman says, the real need of Newfoundland, this measure would do no good at the present time. Since the subject was last before the house I have taken the trouble to discuss this matter with several members of the provincial government, certain officials in Newfoundland, and others who are well acquainted with the power situation in Newfoundland; and I assert without fear of successful contradiction that there is no power available in Newfoundland at the present time that is not committed for consumption at the present time, and that there is in fact a very great power shortage.

May I ask
the hon. member a question?
Yes.
Does he know how many industrial plants started by the Liberal government in Newfoundland have been closed down? Who is using their power now?
I think I am probably as well informed on that subject as is the hon. gentleman. I would not think it would be very relevant to what we are discussing now.

Why did you
make the assertion?

I am dealing with facts, not with hypotheses. The fact is this, and I repeat it; and I suggest that before the hon. gentleman challenges this statement he also get some facts for a change. There is a power shortage in every part of Newfoundland. Does the hon. gentleman think if there were enough hydro power to satisfy St. John's there would be in contemplation at the present time this extension to the thermal plant there? Is the company just doing it for the sake of having it there to look at? Or is it because there is a shortage of power which they want to satisfy?

Atlantic Provinces Power Development
They are expecting a greater expansion of business under a Conservative government.
Oh, oh.

This, Mr. Speaker, from a member of the government that is boasting about the economic pause they have brought about in this country; and I refer to the year end statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I think that economic pause is one of the things we are going to want to get rid of, and that the people of Canada are going to get rid of, along with the government that brought it with them.
They got rid of it last June.
I can well understand why the hon. member for St. John's West wants to bring in these distractions. He does not want his constituents to find out that he was endeavouring to mislead them.
Oh, oh.
Shame.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member would like to let that statement stand.

I would not, Mr. Speaker; Your Honour is perfectly correct. I come back to what I said earlier. I do not think the hon. gentleman would want his constituents to find out that he did not know what this bill was all about. It seems to me that is abundantly clear from what I have already had to say on this subject.
Yesterday the minister boasted, in the usual empty fashion to which we are so accustomed, from the treasury benches, and to which we have been so accustomed since a certain event in December of 1956 when this country was endowed with a new political leader who believes that words are an effective substitute for action-
Look at the record.
I am willing to debate the record with the hon. gentlemen and debate it with them any time they want to do so, but I think Your Honour would not permit me to do it on the discussion of this bill.
Why ask for help?

I do not want any help. Here is what the minister boasted, as reported at page 3307 of Hansard of yesterday:
X think this government has demonstrated its philosophy in listening-[DOT]
That is the first time I ever heard that listening was a philosophy; but as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, there does not seem to be any philosophy here.
-to the wishes of the provinces and in providing what they wanted.

What the government of Newfoundland wants is a small amendment to this bill so we can get something that will give us some cheap power. That is what we want. That is what the premier of Newfoundland asked for last December, and it would have cost this government nothing but perhaps a slight deflation of their pride to accept that request. It is certainly piling on the agony when, after deliberately turning down what was asked for by the provincial government and having the minister from the province say the bill would do something else that the government of the province does not want, the minister then gets to his feet and boasts that they are doing it. It seems to me that this is carrying things rather far.
I think the minister must have made a slip, as I think he will agree if he will look at page 3307 of Hansard. He explained why this bill was limited in the way it is. I think he must have made a slip when he said this:
We wished however to work with the governments of these two provinces of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island in this instance and I think the desire was sincerely indicated and sincerely met.
I am going to be charitable with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and assume that there he meant New Brunswick and Nova Scotia; because there is certainly not the faintest evidence of any kind of any working with the governments of Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. In fact the Prime Minister himself said there would be no truck or trade with those two island provinces unless they made requests, that the federal government did not intend to initiate anything there.

I think the hon. member is being very unfair when he puts in that expression "there would be no truck or trade with those two provinces." That is an interpretation he is putting on which is not justified.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask hon. members to make these corrections and comments at the end of the speech rather than during the course of it.

I thank Your Honour. I should be delighted to have the hon. member for St. John's West, the Minister without Portfolio, rise in his place and join with the Liberal members from Newfoundland in trying to get something for Newfoundland which he is doing his best in one way or another- or seems to be doing his best-to prevent us from getting, or at least to prevent us from asking for.
What did you do about it when you were in office for four years? What did you do to help Newfoundland get electric power?

Well, Mr. Speaker, it
would take more than the 40 minutes which were at my disposal at the beginning of my speech to recount all those things to the hon. gentleman, but I would be happy to do so on another occasion, in the town of Bonavista or in any other place in my riding, if the hon. member knows where those places are.
Does the hon. member not realize that he is the first member speaking in reply to a minister who has moved a government order, and that that carries with it a certain awful right?

I defer to the hon. gentleman's superior knowledge of the rules. I thank him for his friendly interest, and I will relax and avail myself of that right; so hon. gentlemen opposite might just as well begin to possess their souls in patience.
Relax.
And if any hon. member opposite wishes to interrupt me, so long as you permit it, sir, I shall be happy to listen to their interruptions.
We shall accept the invitation.
I am under no restriction whatsoever.
You are very modest.
Oh, yes, I am very modest.
You have a lot to be modest about.

I think that is the hon.
gentleman's first wisecrack in the house, and I give him full marks for it. I am now going to return the courtesy of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre by quoting him from page 3307 of yesterday's Hansard. In a friendly fashion, which I appreciate as a fellow Winnipegger, the hon. member when I had to be elsewhere, as a friend-
A fellow traveller?

-not a political friend but a personal friend-I very much appreciate the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre put this question;
If the aim of the government was to put forward sincere plans meeting the desires of the province of Prince Edward Island and the province of Newfoundland, and in view of the minister's statement that the desire of the government was to meet the wishes of the provincial governments, how does he square that with the refusal of the government to meet Premier Smallwood's request that this bill be amended to provide for assistance in the case of hydroelectric projects?
Atlantic Provinces Power Development
I may say I am very glad that when I was not able to be here the hon. member was good enough to put that question, which I think I would have been the first to put had I been present. Here is the minister's answer;
Mr. Chairman, there is a misunderstanding of the grossest magnitude here. The statement that we have refused Premier Smallwood's request in one sense is true-
This is apparently really "higher philosophy".
-in one sense is true, in so far as a change in this bill to add the word "hydro" is concerned, hut it is certainly not true by any stretch of the imagination to claim that anything we have said or done could be understood to be a refusal of a request to help Newfoundland, either in respect of hydro plants or transmission lines and thermal plants under this particular bill.
I have read that over two or three times this morning and I still cannot find any meaning in it. It appears to be another example of the habit, which is apparently contagious among the few Tories from the province of Saskatchewan, of assuming that words have some connection with deeds. Now to continue the words of the hon. gentleman:
Because this is a matter of vital government policy-
Vital, I believe, means alive. If it is alive why cannot we be told about it? That is what we want to know; just what is this vital policy?
Because this is a matter of vital government policy expressing our point of view to the premier of the province of Newfoundland, a letter will be received soon by the provincial premier expressing our opinion on his wire.
I do not know, sir, whether that means a letter has already been sent. If so, it seems to me that statement constitutes one of the most shocking examples of contempt of parliament I have witnessed since I began looking at this parliament from the galleries 20 years ago. If that letter has been sent on a subject we have been debating in this house for the best part of a week and the hon. gentleman did not communicate its contents to the house, then I would say the rights of members of parliament and particularly those of the opposition are being treated in a fashion which, I believe, even the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would agree never happened under the previous administration.
Don't go too far.

No; I was watching the hon. member's face and my own words very carefully. If this letter has been sent and the minister, in spite of having sent it,

Atlantic Provinces Power Development deliberately refuses-or I should not say deliberately, but he has refused tacitly-to explain his policy to us when we have been asking for it to be explained all along, then as I say that is a simply shocking example of contempt of the rights of parliament.
If, on the other hand, the letter has not been written but this vital policy has come alive-and that is what vital means-then why can we not see it? Are they so ashamed of the little worm that they do not want to expose it to the public gaze? It would appear that the government did not understand, and they did not bother to consult the minister from the province, in fact they have admitted they did not consult the minister from the province about this matter. They did not understand what the government in Newfoundland really wanted and then, having come in to this house without having acceded to the request of the government of Newfoundland, their pride would be hurt if they accepted a suggestion from this side of the house to improve this bill, thereby carrying out what they professed to be the object of the bill, namely to give equal benefits to all the Atlantic provinces.
There does not appear to me to be any reason why even at this late stage either the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources or the Minister without Portfolio- and I say this with regret, but it becomes increasingly clear why that hon. gentleman is Minister without Portfolio-could not get up, as a member of the government, and tell us what is going to be put in the letter to Mr. Smallwood in the event that they have some alternative way of satisfying the needs of Newfoundland which would be satisfactory to that province. However, I suppose this is one of the instances where in the words of their own slogan, they have to "follow John" and they do not know where he is going.
I like Mike.

Furthermore I give the minister full credit for making such a favourable reply and for making it in such categorical terms, but it is precisely because the minister is so definite in respect to the willingness of the government to assist Newfoundland in connection with a hydro project that we made the point that it would be the course of common sense to amend the present bill so that such a request could be made without another bill having to be brought in.
All that needs to be done to the present bill in order to meet such a request from the premier of Newfoundland would be to take the words "by steam driven generators" out of line 16 on page 1 of the bill. There is perhaps one other change which might be considered if Newfoundland were to request assistance in the construction of distribution lines as well as transmission lines and it would simply mean that where the words now read:
Facilities for the control and transmission of electric energy.
3356	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development
They might be changed to read as follows:
Facilities for the control, transmission and distribution of electric energy.
Mr. Speaker, if these two changes were made they would not detract by one iota from the promises made to New Brunswick and to Nova Scotia, but they would widen the terms of the bill so that the government would be in a position to meet a request from Newfoundland for assistance in hydroelectric projects or assistance in the construction of distribution lines which the minister, speaking as a responsible member of the government, has said this government is prepared to meet if such a request comes from the premier or the government of the province of Newfoundland.
Therefore we urge, even at this late stage in the progress of this bill, that the government give consideration to making such an amendment.
I want to say to my hon. friend and fellow Winnipegger, the member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate-and I appreciate his reference to me this morning as a fellow Winnipegger-that if I were a member for a Newfoundland constituency, as he is, I think I would have done something other than speak for a full hour today and let it go at that. He had the right this morning to speak without time limit and he almost did it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He did. He took an hour and a half.

But
he also had another right of which he did not avail himself and I remind him of this now because there are other Newfoundland members in the house and I gather one or two of them may yet be speaking in this debate and perhaps they can do what he failed to do.
Actually if the members from Newfoundland, want, in the words of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, to do the most effective thing they can do to extend this bill to all four of the Atlantic provinces, they should be moving an amendment. It is a very simple one and if they would like it I will draft it for them. I do not want to take this away from them because after all I still live in Winnipeg, but my friend of the old days in the United College has gone down to our tenth province-
He has gone down.

-and it seems to me that if any amendment with regard to this matter is going to be moved he or one of his colleagues from the province of Newfoundland should move it. I will tell him what the words are and he can take them down and perhaps the member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) or the


member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) or the member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) or even the member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne)-
Or St. John's East (Mr. McGrath).

Yes
-may wish to move it and I will give it to them without any copyright or any charge whatsoever.
In other words, the member for Bonavista-Twillingate could, if he had really wanted to take some action on this instead of merely speaking for an hour, have simply stood up and moved that Bill No. 244 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of re-considering the provisions of clause 2 (d) and clause 3 (1) thereof.
I remind my hon. friend that if he was reluctant to move such an amendment because he was afraid it would be regarded as a motion of want of confidence in the government-I do not know why he would be reluctant to do that-but just in case that was the reason, that he wanted to speak at length-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: A very appropriate day.

-rather than move an amendment, may I remind him that this question was answered last night. I drew the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to the fact that a companion bill to this one-the Beechwood bill-ran into a procedural vote over in the other place and, believe it or not, the Liberals stood up and voted, defeating the Tories on this matter in the Senate. I asked the Minister of Finance if that was a defeat of the government and he said "No", that it was only a procedural matter over in the other place.
That makes it pretty clear that if all we had now was a procedural proposal to refer this bill back to committee to reconsider the clauses in which power projects are defined it would not be a vote of non-confidence in the government. In fact Newfoundland members on the Conservative side of the house could vote for it and that would give us the chance of making this bill what the title says it is supposed to be, the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act.
I will give the amendment free of charge to any Newfoundlander, Liberal or Tory, who wants to move it on behalf of his province. I think the right thing to do is to appeal to the government even yet to take this bill back into committee and to strike out the words "by steam driven generators" so that

this bill will in tact as well as in name be a basis of providing assistance to the economy of all four of the Atlantic provinces of this country.
Mr. Speaker,-

Do
you not want this amendment?
Go on take it.

I am not sure that any decision arrived at in the other place would be regarded as a precedent for this chamber, and in any case I think the hon) member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would agree we did move an amendment to this legislation, and that we did not have much success with it.
Yours was out of order.
The hon. gentleman did not think so.

The
chairman did.
The hon. gentleman maintained that the amendment we moved was in order. We on this side of the house have established a reputation of abiding by the rulings of the chair.
Since when?

I think the government now realizes that they made a mistake when they introduced this legislation as part of a national policy. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, not only is it not a national policy but it does not even represent a policy for the Atlantic provinces. What this legislation is, is special legislation for two maritime provinces. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) let the cat out of the bag when he spoke yesterday as reported on page 3320 of Hansard and said:
I think I have made it clear once or twice before but in so far as hydro plants in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are concerned-I am speaking of one in particular-it was at the insistence of the premiers of these provinces that these hydro projects were kept out of this bill. This matter was discussed between the two premiers and myself. Possibly X would have advanced the same argument as my hon. [DOT] friend had it not been for the insistence of the two premiers.
I think that proves conclusively that this legislation was never intended to be part of a national policy, and was never intended to benefit any of the maritime provinces except the two provinces to which the minister referred when he made that statement. If the government had wanted to bring in a national policy, the proper method of doing 96698-213J
Atlantic Provinces Power Development it would have been, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has so clearly stated, to have moved an amendment to existing legislation which is already on the statute books and which would require only a simple amendment to permit agreements with the provinces concerned. The minister has admitted that a separate bill must be brought in in respect of every province that wishes to make an agreement, under the present arrangements, and surely it is not good legislation to be cluttering up the statute books with eight, nine or ten bills when a simple amendment to an existing one would be sufficient.
We have been told by the minister and also by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) that the most Newfoundland can expect to get from this legislation is assistance in the construction of transmission lines, and from an earlier statement the minister made on second reading, and which he repeated on the resolution stage, this is something he envisages might take place at some time in the far distant future. The terms of the bill do look far into the future, because I see it sets a period of 30 years and sometimes 40 years for the repayment of funds under this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question? Am I to assume that he is saying we are not willing to help the thermal plant at St. John's.

It is not at all clear what assistance the thermal plant at St. John's could get from this measure because that plant is privately owned, as I understand it, and I notice that last night, in reply to a question which the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) asked at my request, the minister was very vague as to the basis on which any subvention would be paid on coal consumed in thermal plants in Newfoundland. The question of water transportation charges was also brought up and the minister carefully avoided it on the grounds that it was a hypothetical question and, also, when he was asked on what basis cost would be equalized-whether the cost of coal used in thermal plants in Newfoundland would be equalized with the cost of coal in a similar plant in New Brunswick-the minister again gave an evasive answer.
So we are still waiting for the minister to tell us what assistance we can hope to get from this act, other than assistance in the construction of transmission lines. Even this is something that is envisaged only in the dim and distant future. If we are going to look into the future, I think we should take into consideration the statement made
3358	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) on January 9, as reported on page 3100 of Hansard. The hon. member for Vancouver East, who is something of an authority on matters of this kind because he is an electrician by trade, told us that the methods of transmission of electricity are undergoing very rapid change. He said, and I am quoting now from page 3100:
In electricity, today is not yesterday. Today not only are we changing from copper to aluminum above ground but the same thing applies to undersea cables. In the past they were seventy-two thousand volts and 220,000 volts but now they are 750,000 volts, and this has changed the complete idea of the distribution of electricity. Therefore, it might be better to produce electricity 750 miles away and distribute it.
Thus, at the rapid rate at which technological progress is taking place, I think that before 30 years are over it is safe to assume that not even this kind of cable will be in use but that, possibly, electricity will be transmitted from some huge generator such as might be located on the Grand falls of the Hamilton river in Labrador and transmitted from there, possibly by radiation. Would it be wise for any private company to commit itself to huge expenditures on transmission lines which might become obsolete before they could become fully amortized?
On second reading I pointed out that this bill could have a serious effect on the fishing industry in my province and particularly on the processing phase of that industry. 1 pointed out that efforts were being made to develop our salt fish and our fresh fish industry in Newfoundland in order to provide employment for our increasing population. I pointed out also that we were in direct competition with plants producing a similar product in Nova Scotia, and that Nova Scotia already enjoyed certain advantages with regard to transportation and amortization costs which are much lower than those we have to face in Newfoundland. These are two distinct advantages which Nova Scotia possesses over Newfoundland. Now the federal government by means of this legislation is making a direct intervention in private enterprise, and is providing assistance to fish processors on the mainland which it is denying to similar processors in Newfoundland. That could have two effects, and neither of them would be very satisfactory.
One effect could be to put the fish processing plant in such a position that it could stay in business and compete with Nova Scotia plants only by lowering the price paid to our fishermen for their fish, and goodness knows that price is already too low, and far below a subsistence level. The other effect could be even worse, because it could put our


Newfoundland plants out of business altogether and that would mean that Newfoundland fishermen would be condemned by this legislation to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for fish plants in Nova Scotia.

Mr. Speaker, I hope my remarks on third reading of this bill will be brief. Yesterday in my absence certain statements were put on the record by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) and by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks), to which I should like to reply briefly.
The one point I hope to be able to make is this. It would appear to me that there has been an effort in this house to try to convince members on this side and the citizens of New Brunswick that what is before the house now, and the bill that was passed a few days ago, mean cheap power for the province of New Brunswick. I believe we must all agree that the project with which we dealt the other day, and this project, do not mean cheap power to the province of New Brunswick. We must recognize that fact. In speaking yesterday the Minister of Veterans Affairs had this to-say, as reported at page 3301 of Hansard:
The reasons given for this discrepancy were the fact that the maritimes lacked industry and that our transportation system worked to the detriment of the development of those provinces. Many reports have been made on this subject including the Duncan report and more recent ones which indicated two important reasons for the failure of the maritime provinces to keep abreast of the development in the other provinces. The first reason was the lack of cheap power to develop industries and the second was the high cost of transportation in the maritime provinces.
The minister did not say there that this is cheap power but implied that this development in New Brunswick means cheap power. I can go back to the submission which was made to the government in 1956, in which it very plainly points out that
50,000	kilowatt thermal plants in New Brunswick, burning bunker oil can develop power for exactly the same price as it is estimated the Beechwood power will cost. It certainly is not cheap power, and I feel the people of the province should know that it is not cheap power, because when this program has been completed and put into operation in New Brunswick it will still not provide cheap power.
During his remarks yesterday the hon. member for Royal made another statement to which I wish to refer. He referred to me and he said, as reported at page 3302 of Hansard:
The other day the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) complained because Grand falls in New Brunswick was developing power for private concerns. I might point out to the house that in

Atlantic Provinces Power Development
Newfoundland about 95 per cent of the power produced is produced by private companies. Those private companies are willing to develop electric power from the rivers, and so on.
When I referred to the Grand falls project the other day, the hon. member for Royal interrupted me and said that my reference to Grand falls was not correct. My reference to Grand falls was to the effect that in 1925 the engineering work in connection with Grand falls had been completed; the storage rights had been obtained from the state of Maine and the province of Quebec. Tenders had been called to complete the power project. It was estimated at that time that it would cost $10 million and would provide
380,000	horsepower in the province of New Brunswick, much greater than any single development anywhere else in the maritime provinces. But when the provincial government changed in 1926-the Minister of Veterans Affairs was a member of the provincial legislature at that time-they decided not to go ahead with that project. It was sold to the Gatineau Power Company and the project was built and has been operated and maintained by the Gatineau Power Company ever since. I said the other day, and I repeat, that the development of electrical energy in my province was retarded for 10 or 15 years by the action of the provincial government of that day. That is why we are power-hungry to the extent that we are at the present time.
I do hope that my friends from Newfoundland will gain some consideration for the plea that they have put up in this house. I must agree that if the matter was reversed, if this assistance was to be provided for the province of Newfoundland and we in the province of New Brunswick were to be ignored, I would use exactly the same tactics in presenting my views to the House of Commons as have been used today by the members from Newfoundland. I believe they have every right to expect that any assistance that is provided for one of the Atlantic provinces should be provided for all four.
I just wish to mention an idea that I have thought a lot about recently and during this discussion. Someone asked a question this morning-I think it was of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who was speaking at the time-whether he thought thermal plants could be developed successfully in Newfoundland. I think that was a most reasonable question to ask. We all know that they just do not mine any coal in Newfoundland. They are in this position. If they were to develop thermal power, whatever fuel would be used would have to be taken there by water and in some instances at great distances.
A few years ago the federal government decided to go ahead with some experimenting in the development of power from atomic energy. After several months of consultation with the provinces, the province of Ontario agreed to go in with the federal government, together with the General Electric Company of Canada, to experiment with an atomic energy station here in Ontario. I believe that station has been in the process of building for about two years. I think it will be completed sometime next year. I would think that in Newfoundland there is a great possibility of carrying out such a development. We would get away from the transportation of fuel which costs an enormous amount to start with. If there is one place in Canada where atomic energy might be taken into consideration as a power development it is in the province of Newfoundland. I hope the government will give consideration to this, if they are able to obtain full information as to the progress made in the development here in Ontario and the prospects for the future.
I wanted to point these things out to the minister, to the house and to the people in my province to show that this development, or any other development that has been suggested in this house in the past six months, in no way will decrease the cost of electrical energy by one cent to the domestic users in the province of New Brunswick. Some sort of an arrangement or agreement may be worked out whereby industry might be able to get power at some reduction, but there is no indication on the part of the provincial government, when this program is completed, of a cut in the cost of electrical energy to the domestic users in my province.
Before I resume my seat I again wish to emphasize the fact that in no way will this plan-I endorse it; it is a help to my province-produce cheap power because cheap power just cannot be produced in this way. You cannot produce cheap power from coal; you cannot produce cheap power from oil. As far as the development of hydro power is concerned, in the submission made to the provincial government-I know the minister has a copy of it-the admission is made that in order to develop Beechwood, to borrow money at five per cent means energy at seven mills.
Right after that they say they can build
50,000	kilowatt thermal plants burning bunker oil and develop power for seven mills. So hydro power is no cheaper than thermal power, and in my estimation and I believe the estimation of most people in my province that this plan or any other plan we have
3360	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development ever had under consideration will not produce cheap energy for the province of New Brunswick.

Mr. Speaker, we have come to the final stage of this 'bill and in the final stage I must, as I did on the resolution stage and on second reading, make my plea to the minister to amend the bill so that the benefits which will accrue to the provinces of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia will also accrue to the people of the province of Newfoundland. I say again, sir, as I have said on two previous occasions, that I am going to support the bill. To do otherwise would be to deny to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island the very advantages which I now seek for my own province.
In talking the way that Newfoundland members on this side of the house have talked, I do not want to leave the impression that there is very little electrical development in Newfoundland because such would not be the case. In the report of th dominion bureau of statistics for the month of August, 1957 figures are given as to the totals generated by the provinces for the month of August 1957. The total for Nova Scotia was approximately 120 million kilowatt hours, for New Brunswick 115 million kilowatt hours, for Prince Edward Island 5 million kilowatt hours and for Newfoundland 103 million kilowatt hours. We do have considerable electrical development in Newfoundland but not nearly enough to satisfy our needs.
As I have said before, our development in Newfoundland is specifically of the hydro type and we still have sufficient water power available there to supply Newfoundland with the electrical energy that it will need for some time to come. This cannot be said for the other three provinces. I have made some rough calculations from figures I have been able to obtain. It appears that of the amount of energy that has been developed over the last few years in the province of New Brunswick 60 per cent has been produced by thermal power and 40 per cent by hydro power. In the province of Nova Scotia 75 per cent has been produced by thermal power and 25 per cent by hydro power. In the province of Prince Edward Island not all but pretty nearly 100 per cent of the electricity used is produced by thermal plants. But in the province of Newfoundland over 92 per cent of the electrical energy used is produced by hydro developments.
In my own area of Humber-St. George's there is considerable development in the town of Deer Lake, 30 miles from the city of Corner Brook. We have there the great Bowater project which develops slightly over
[Mr. Stuart (Charlotte) .1

150,000	horsepower. This electrical energy is used by the great newsprint mills at Corner Brook, by other settlements in the vicinity and also by the mining town of Buchan's, but sufficient energy is not produced to be able to service those parts of my riding which are far south or far north of the central point where the electricity is produced. At St. George's there is another small plant which last year produced approximately 17 million kilowatt hours.
In the other stages of the debate I have not referred specifically very often to parts of my riding but on this occasion I will. I say to the minister that in Newfoundland we have always been hampered by two great problems. One is the problem of transportation and the other is the problem of electrical power. We have been able to do something about transportation and I think improvements are being made all the time. When a year ago the minister of finance of that time, Mr. Harris, spoke in his budget speech about what was going to be done for the maritime provinces with regard to electrical power I thought that here was a chance for my province to be able to find some remedy for a festering sore that has hampered it for years. We also hoped that when this bill was brought forward it would do something for the province of Newfoundland but I think that the wording of it discriminates against us and I do not see how we are going to receive any benefit from this legislation at all.
In the southern part of my riding, from the town of St. George's up to Cape Ray, all along the Codroy valley, we have a very large area, large for Newfoundland, of very fertile land, possibly the best farming land in the province of Newfoundland. Here we have a large number of farmers who are operating their farms without the use of electricity. We import into Newfoundland every year large quantities of farm produce which we could easily grow ourselves. The farming industry in western Newfoundland would receive a shot in the arm if we were able to provide these people with electrical power.
We can go down to the Codroy valley. Here in one of the most scenic spots in eastern Canada we would be able to develop one of the finest tourist industries. Yet here we are trying to struggle along without the benefits of electrical power.
I wonder whether I could ask the hon. gentleman a question.

Certainly.

Atlantic Provinces Power Development

Is it not a
fact that the United Towns Electric Company generates and transmits electricity in the St. George's area?

I am referring to the area west of St. George's, between St. George's and Cape Ray in the Codroy valley. The company to which the hon. member refers does not transmit electricity in that area. In the last year or two it has serviced the area around Port au Port but west of St. George's it does not service the area. Those people are entirely without any service so far as electric power is concerned except what they can develop with their own small engines or in other ways. As I was saying, in the Codroy valley, one of the most scenic spots in eastern Canada where a fine tourist industry could be developed, the people are trying to struggle along without the advantages that would come to them if they had electric power.
On both sides of the great Codroy river there are many settlements that would benefit greatly if they were serviced with this form of energy. There are large tracts of good land. At Codroy harbour there is a fine fishing centre which we hope will some time be the centre of a fish plant and bait depot that will service the fishermen along the coast. I cannot see how all this is going to be done in an efficient manner without electrical power.
I could go on to bay of Islands, both on the north side and the south side, where there are some of the finest fishing settlements on the Atlantic seaboard. What advantages would come to these people if they could have the benefit of electrical power! I could go on to beautiful Bonne bay, a real tourist attraction. Here again these people are not serviced by electrical power.
I appeal again to the minister to reconsider the bill and to give the people who live in Newfoundland the same advantages as will be given to the people of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. I am not going to move an amendment but I am going to appeal to the minister's good judgment. Let me close by saying that the bill as it now stands refers to thermal power and will be accepted by the people of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, but I wonder how they would feel if instead of the word "thermal" the word "hydro" had been used in the bill? They would argue that because the word "hydro" was used those provinces could not get the best advantage out of the legislation because in order for them to have electrical power it must be produced by thermal plants. We are in exactly the same position. I would think if the legislation were rewritten and the word
"hydro" was used instead of "thermal it would pose a very serious problem to the provinces of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this bill as it reads now, containing only the word "thermal", imposes the same problem on the province of Newfoundland. Once again may I appeal to the minister and ask if he will reconsider the wording of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take about five minutes to present some matters, and in doing so I shall stay within the scope of this bill. However, I understand that when a bill comes up for third reading an hon. member who is in favour of it make take that opportunity to make some recommendations to the government and that is what I propose to do. There are three reasons why I rise at this time. First, I should like to put on the record some remarks which appear in the speech from the throne. I should like to read a particular sentence which appears at page 6 of Hansard of October 14, 1957:
My ministers believe that a national development policy carried out in co-operation with the provinces, and in the territories, is needed to enable all regions of Canada to share in the benefits to be realized in developing the resources of this great nation.
My second reason for rising is that I wanted to make a special appeal at the resolution stage, and I was unable to be present. I want to thank my colleague, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill) for having spoken on my behalf at that time.
My third reason for rising is that I should like to put on the record remarks made by Premier Campbell of Manitoba at the dominion-provincial conference held in Ottawa on November 25 and 26, 1957. I shall just quote two paragraphs:
One important remaining area where such a national development policy could be applied is in the electrical power field. In the entire southern half of our country a rapid growth in power requirements has almost exhausted nearby sources of hydroelectric power and is forcing many areas to consider a much greater use of thermal power. Yet the northern half of Canada still has very substantial hydroelectric power potentials. One has only to mention Mica creek, Frobisher and the Rocky mountain trench in British Columbia, the North Saskatchewan river in Alberta and Saskatchewan, the Nelson and Churchill rivers in Manitoba, the numerous streams running into Hudson's bay in Ontario and Quebec, and the Hamilton river in Labrador, to emphasize the truth of this statement.
The other paragraph which I should like to put on the record is as follows:
A number of these northern power sites involve very large expenditures in the construction of dams and other facilities, and consideration should
3362	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development be given to the possibility of providing federal assistance for these very costly projects during the early load-building period. In this connection Manitoba has noted with interest the recent announcement concerning federal aid to the Beech-wood project in New Brunswick, the South Saskatchewan dam in Saskatchewan and also the statement of government policy regarding the Mica creek project in British Columbia. We assume that similar federal assistance will be available for projects under way or soon to be undertaken in Manitoba.
Those are all the remarks that I wanted to make, but I did want to have them on the record.

I have a few comments to make, but I shall be brief because I just wish to discuss the principle of this bill, and particularly the policy of the government as expressed in this particular bill. It would seem to me that the government is being true to its traditions in this particular bill by operating on a regional basis. Their outlook has always been regional and sectional, and possibly that is the reason why their support has been on that same basis over a period of years, until just recently when, as a result of a sufficient lapse of time, the people had forgotten these grand Tory policies.
I wonder if the minister will not tell us before the bill is passed, having some regard for those people who sent him here, that he is going to extend the same privileges to the people in Saskatchewan with regard to power as he is providing in this very narrow bill. In other words, I am asking the Conservative party if they will not extend their policy and put it on more of a national basis instead of a regional and sectional one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. We are now considering third reading of this bill. This is a bill dealing with the development of power in the Atlantic provinces. He proceeds now to ask questions of the minister. He must realize that the proper time to put questions to the minister was at the committee stage. The bill was reported by the committee yesterday.
We are not dealing with a broad question of national policy, Mr. Speaker, as applied to the west. We are dealing with a particular bill, the principle of which has been approved already by the house on second reading. The bill has already been reported back to the house. In my respectful submission, speeches of this kind are entirely out of order at this stage.

is quite evident that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is anxious, at every stage of this bill, to prevent any debate which would make it possible to compare one project proposed by the government with another. It does seem to me, sir-

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege.

I am rising on a question of privilege. It seems to me that it ill becomes the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), who was often accorded the courtesy in the previous parliament of having government business put over to suit his convenience and that of his colleagues when they were on this side of the house, to make any such imputation, and I would request the hon. gentleman to withdraw it.

Having had that delightful excursion into histrionics, Mr. Speaker, perhaps we can come back to the matter before the house for a moment or two, because I intend to speak only for a few minutes on it. The hon. member for Charlotte made a reference to this bill in which he said it would not be of any direct advantage to the domestic user of electric energy in the maritime provinces. I think that is a fair statement. I think it is a correct statement, according to my understanding of the-bill. This bill is designed to enable cheaper power to be produced in the Atlantic provinces for power use or for the consumption of power. It does not have any reference to the development of power for domestic purposes.
In the maritimes-and I presume in Newfoundland as well, although I cannot speak with the knowledge that I can of the other three provinces-the cry throughout our lifetime, as the hon. member for Charlotte well knows, has been that we need more industry. We need industrial development in those provinces, and industrial development has not been proceeded with because we have not had the power potential or at least the power development in order to attract those industries to those provinces. This bill is therefore designed to provide that government assistance is given to it so that power may be purchased more cheaply, and that power will be used for industrial purposes in the maritime provinces. There is no question that the criticism-if it were a criticism-of the hon. member for Charlotte is justified. But I say it is not

a criticism. It is something to the bill's credit. Certainly the people in the maritime provinces will be very happy-I refer to the domestic consumers-to pay the domestic rates which they pay now if they can see an industrial development taking place in those provinces as those of us who have studied this bill, who have worked for it and have dreamed about it, can see taking place in those provinces. With that industrial development there will come, of course, a reduction in the cost of domestic power as well. So much for that matter.
A great deal has been said by our friends from Newfoundland about this bill. Frankly, I cannot quite understand the position which they take. They say that Newfoundland is prejudiced by this bill, and that it is discriminatory.
Who said that?

The hon. member who just sat down. I think I am paraphrasing him correctly. Certainly the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) said that the fish processors of Newfoundland were going to be prejudiced because Nova Scotia apparently could get cheaper power. All sorts of statements such as that one have been made which I do not think have any foundation in fact, and are maybe only fancy, Mr. Speaker, very fanciful fancy at that.
It is rather refreshing, shall I say-or is it disconcerting-to sit here in this house and listen to the pathetic pleas of the former cabinet minister, the member from Newfoundland, who spoke for one and a half hours this morning, regretting how this government was prejudicing that beloved province of his, Newfoundland, by what we are doing to it. What are we doing, Mr. Speaker?
Refusing the request of the provincial government.

What we are doing is improving, amplifying and developing the electric power of the province, a course which was hinted at by the previous government of which the hon. gentleman was a member. In 1948 the Liberal party at its national convention brought forward a plan urging the development of power in the Atlantic provinces and in the election of 1953 they enlightened the people of the maritimes with respect to what they hoped to do in principle.
I remember the remarks of the late Angus L. Macdonald on what was going to happen but the election of 1953 was well advanced when the former government suddenly realized they were facing a disastrous defeat in the maritime provinces. At that time the former minister of finance pulled a rabbit out of his hat one night-an infant rabbit, not
