"We are going to produce power at cost"-whatever that was. Coal was not to be assisted; there was no assistance to be given to coal.
That is not correct.

There was no information with respect to that. We asked how he defined costs and we were told that could not be done. We asked who was to own the plants and we were told the federal government was going to own them. We were going to have a competing system of ownership. This was the plan for the maritime provinces but it was a system for New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and there was no reference to Prince Edward Island in that. Nor was there any reference to Newfoundland in that.
This is the gentleman who now weeps such copious tears because this government has produced a plan which is workable and which will mean a tremendous development in the maritimes. He says we have overlooked Newfoundland. He forgot Newfoundland when he was in the cabinet.
I wonder where in Hansard during the eight years he sat here as a member of the government-I think it was eight years but perhaps it was more-we could find one word from the hon. gentleman as either the secretary of state or afterwards the minister of citizenship and immigration mentioning power development in Newfoundland. I wonder where we could find one word from any of the other members from Newfoundland who have today spoken on this matter. After all they sat in the house for four years, some of them for eight years.
Nine years.

Yes. They never thought of power in Newfoundland then; all they thought of was hiding behind the skirts of the secretary of state who was later the minister of citizenship and immigration. He did not think of power so they did not think of power. That is all there was to it.
In speaking on Newfoundland I am reminded of the speech of the former secretary of state made, I think in the debate on the address, in which he made some rather caustic references, or "sympathetic" references, to my colleague from Newfoundland, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Browne). He again wept bitter tears for Newfoundland, that dear province which is so down-trodden and oppressed by the Tories because all we did was appoint a cabinet minister without

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I believe a moment or two ago I was interrupted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on a point of order relating to the fact that I might have been wandering a little bit from the restrictive part of this particular measure. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. minister to confine his remarks to the bill.
I thank the hon. gentleman for writing my election manifesto.

One other reference I should like to make is to the suggestions made by hon. members, including I think the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson), that this bill was too restrictive. Mr. Speaker, this undoubtedly is not the only bill which will be introduced dealing with power development in Canada as the years go by. The mere fact that this bill is related to the Atlantic provinces does not mean other bills will not be introduced and undoubtedly this government in the years which lie ahead of us


will have ample opportunity to bring in legislation to deal with power development in other parts of Canada.
Meanwhile we wait.
Is the hon. minister intimating that the government is contemplating passing legislation to give federal assistance to projects in northern Manitoba?

I am intimating nothing except that this is not the only bill which will be introduced in the House of Commons by the Conservative government in the future. There will be lots of opportunity, but unfortunately some members who are asking these questions about it today will not be here to see these bills introduced. However, they can read about them in the newspapers.
Is that a threat?

I can assure them this will be done because this is another one of the specific pledges which were made in the last election. We were faced with this half baked, hair brained scheme which was proposed at that moment-a deathbed repentence on the part of the former government-and we had to deal with it. We promised at that time that if the Conservative government was elected a bill would be introduced to provide for assistance in the way of subvention on coal and development of thermal power within the maritime provinces. That was a specific election pledge given by the then leader of the opposition and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) supported by every one of the ten Conservative members from Nova Scotia and those from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. It was also supported by the premiers of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and it is in furtherance of that pledge that this bill has been introduced.
Let me say that when this pledge was made, frankly the thinking was directed primarily towards coal for the development of thermal power and perhaps was centred on New Brunswick and Nova Scotia with transmission lines to Prince Edward Island. It was due to the urging of the hon. members from Newfoundland, my colleague in the cabinet and the other member for St. John's that Newfoundland was included in this bill. Instead of being criticized and instead of it being stated that they failed in their duty, they deserve the thanks of the people of Newfoundland for the fact that we now have a balanced bill dealing with the Atlantic provinces.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this bill will shortly be passed and that when it is, within a very short time, the effects of his bill will

make a greater imprint upon the industrial development and the future of the maritime provinces than has any other piece of legislation which has been passed by a government of Canada in the last 20 years.

Will the Minister of National Revenue permit a question before he sits down? Perhaps he will allow me to ask him a question, since the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has declined the offer to say a few words by unanimous consent.
Is it not a fact that the bill as drafted makes available to the Atlantic provinces a type of assistance which Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are in a position to take but which the province of Newfoundland is not in a position to take; and would it be doing any harm to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick -would it be breaking faith in any way- if the bill were broadened in order that the assistance proposed in this bill might be available in practical terms to all four Atlantic provinces?

I do not think any harm would be done to Nova Scotia or New Brunswick if this were widened, though I am not prepared to pass judgment on that point. This bill has been a subject of almost constant discussion by responsible ministers, by a subcommittee of the cabinet and by officials for four or five months. Within a month after taking office, some of us set the machinery in motion-
It was already in motion.

It was not in motion; it was in reverse. And after all these discussions, after all the preliminary work has been done, certainly I would not want to be in a position-and I do not think the government would, either,-of introducing substantial changes in legislation which has arisen out of constant co-operation and study between the governments concerned. As far as I know, the premier of Newfoundland has not even asked for the benefits of this bill to be extended to Newfoundland. There will be ample time in the future for that. This government will be here for a long time- probably longer than the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate or the premier of Newfoundland

and we will be able to deal with this question in the future. The important thing now is to get this bill through.

Can
the minister say whether the letter which has been written to the premier of Newfoundland has been mailed to him, or taken to him up in the gallery? If so, can he say whether a copy of that letter will be tabled in this house?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I feel there is not a great deal I should say at this time in introducing the estimates. I am prepared to answer fully and in such detail as may be desired any questions that may be asked, but it is my hope that we will be able to deal with the estimates efficiently and expeditiously. We have seen in the course of the last few hours and, indeed, in the course of the last few days an attempt to delay matters by what I may call a pickersgilli-buster, and for my part I do not intend to do anything which would hold up these estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire whatsoever to delay the passage of
33C8	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the estimates, about three quarters or four-fifths of which-I have not done the addition lately as between the original estimates and the supplementaries-were presented to the previous parliament on my recommendation.
One observation I should like to make at the outset is that whatever waste or extravagance the Minister of Finance might have found in other departments it is abundantly clear he has found none in this department, because he has asked for an increase of 20 or 25 per cent in estimates which Mr. Harris laid before the house in the last parliament. This, I believe, is the biggest increase which has been asked for by any department in percentage terms. I regard that as a tribute to the economy, the efficiency and perhaps, almost, to the parsimoniousness with which the department was administered under a Liberal administration.
I intend just the same to put to the minister the question which we have put to every other minister at some stage during his estimates, and ask him to tell us whether he or the Minister of Finance has in fact found any waste or extravagance in this department. I rather think the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will tell us frankly or in a straightforward way, as is his custom -I might add, a refreshing custom. Because it is becoming increasingly clear that the famous statement made to the Canadian Press last June by the Minister of Finance when he told us he was going to bring down a budget, which has never been brought down, and when he made a lot of other extravagant claims that look pretty sick in the cold light of a January day-the statement that boasts that after a few days in office the Minister of Finance had found a great deal of waste and extravagance in almost every one of the departments, cannot be substantiated today. Now that a great deal of time has elapsed and many of the departments concerned have been under examination, we have not had a single minister who could give us a single example of any kind of waste or extravagance which has been found in his department.
Indeed, this government which boasted it could reduce the expenditures of this country by half a billion dollars has been adding to the expenditure of practically every department; and in those rare cases where it has produced what looks like a decrease, at first flush or, at any rate, no increase, it has done so by a process of legerdemain by deferring certain expenditure in order to carry on other expenditure without increasing the aggregate expenditure of the department.


I know that if I had stayed in office after June 21 I would have had to go to the minister of finance and ask for an increase in the estimates just as the hon. gentleman did. I know I would have had to do it because there was a most unprecedented development during the course of the year after the estimates had been prepared which involved expenditures which were really quite impossible accurately to estimate at the time the regular estimates, or even the supplementary estimates that were brought down before the end of the last parliament, were prepared.
As I said, when the Minister of Finance asked for interim supply on October 17, and when I made certain observations about the very large increase in the estimates being asked for by the present minister-I think, sir, I will call him the present minister and not the acting minister, for convenience-if I had to pick a successor in his party I could not wish for a better one. I think the minister, as I said earlier, is the ablest member of this government by a very considerable margin. I would like to repeat what I said this morning, I could not pay him any higher compliment than to say that if he shared some Liberal ideas, if he did not have those old-fashioned Tory notions, which I outgrew at an early age and which he has not outgrown, I would be quite happy to see the hon. gentleman in a Liberal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman trying to blight my prospects?

The hon. gentleman would not expect me to do anything inside the house to improve them and he perhaps would not expect me to do much outside the house to help him along the road; but I must say, sir, that if we must have the misfortune of a Tory government there is no one I would rather see in it than the hon. gentleman. I must add to that, sir, that if in a Tory government I had to see at the head of a department in which I took a great interest-and I am sure the minister would admit that I did -a Tory minister there is no one in the house I would rather see administer it than the hon. gentleman. I say that, in part, because he has paid me the very great compliment-not to me only, but to my predecessor, Mr. Harris, who really in the pioneering days of this department did lay down policies and procedures in which I found very little to change -of carrying on those policies and procedures almost precisely as they were carried on prior to June 21.
There were times when the hon. gentleman was on this side of the house when he was- and I do not criticize him for that-perhaps somewhat extravagant in his criticism of things he did not entirely understand at that

time, but which 1 think he understands much better now. But the hon. gentleman has, as I say, followed the procedures and policies in the main that were followed before.
I have no doubt the hon. gentleman will tell us that he is giving study to the very important legislation he is responsible for administering, in addition to another very heavy portfolio, and that he could not be expected, as an acting minister, to make sudden and drastic changes. I am going to suggest that if things had been anything like as bad as the hon. gentleman used to say they were, that would be a very poor excuse. But the fact is they were not and the hon. gentleman quite sensibly has found they were not; he has found that there was a good reason for practically everything that was done in the department and he has gone on doing those things as far as I have been able to learn-* and I have made some inquiries through the channels open to us in the opposition by putting questions on the order paper, and the answers I have received have been of the most reassuring character-in the same way.
I think the committee will be interested -I know I would be greatly interested-if the hon. gentleman, when he does rise to speak, would tell us specifically and concretely one by one precisely what changes he has made in policy or in procedures. I want to admit that there is in the department -anyone will admit it-in its policies in some regards, and in procedures in others, always room for change and always room for improvement. I think the hon. gentleman would not deny that when I was minister, even though it was a very good department and very well administered when I became minister on July 1, 1954, I did make some changes which were improvements. I think particularly of the arrangement for the citizenship courts in Toronto and Montreal. A situation had developed there where because of the divided jurisdiction and divided responsibility a most unreasonable time elapsed between an application for citizenship and the granting of the citizenship. The conditions in the court in the city hall in Toronto at the time I visited it not long after I became minister really shocked me profoundly.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Most certainly.

Since the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate seems to be very favourably impressed with the administration of the department under the former government, would he care to comment upon the regulation, which I believe
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration was put into effect under his jurisdiction, whereby a resident of Canada might be refused citizenship-

I do not think the former minister is under review at this particular time.
He has to learn.

Since I came into this house four and one-half years ago I have prided myself on never declining to listen to and try to answer any question that any hon. member addressed to me, and though perhaps the hon. gentleman's question, as you have indicated, sir, is a little bit out of order, I would have been prepared, with the indulgence of the committee, to answer it; but since the hon. member for Kamloops is now the minister in charge of the department perhaps it might more properly be directed to him.
Perhaps I might continue with the train of thought which the hon. member interrupted. I would like to conclude what I had to say about the court in Toronto which granted citizenship before the federal court was established. I said at the time the change was made, and I repeat, I did not want to blame anyone for it. I did not think anyone was subject to blame. It was one of those cases where a court was run in the city hall by the provincial government, where it was serving a purpose that was primarily federal and where the divided jurisdiction was not satisfactory. I am happy to say that up to June 21 we had had the greatest satisfaction with the federal court in Toronto and also with the court in Montreal, and I have no reason to think that both those courts are not performing in the same satisfactory way today.
I have had the feeling for some time that there were one or two other spots in Canada where the courts which had to do with applications for citizenship were not functioning very satisfactorily. I know I had the greatest difficulty over the situation in New Brunswick and when the minister replies I should like him to tell me whether it has been possible for him to improve the situation in that province. I understand the matter was taken up by the local citizenship councils who were just as shocked as I was in discovering some of the practices that were going on in those courts. It was one of those things to which I had planned to give attention if I had remained in charge of the department.
I do think it is of the utmost importance that the federal government do everything that it is possible to do to make the formal granting of citizenship and the carrying on
3370	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of these ceremonies in the citizenship courts as dignified and as impressive as possible. I said in the house once, I think, that for many of those receiving citizenship it was the greatest occasion next to marriage. I did try, and I got a good deal of co-operation from members in all parties in the house, to encourage the courts to make these ceremonies as impressive as possible, but I always maintained it would be unreasonable to establish federal courts all over the country because the number of citizenship cases that arise, for example, in the province of Newfoundland, if I dare mention that province again today-it does not receive a large number of immigrants-would certainly not warrant the appointment of a special judge to deal with them. That would be true of all the Atlantic provinces. It would be true of most of the rural parts of Quebec, in fact, many of the rural sections of other parts of Canada. I am sure the present minister is finding the same difficulty I found in attracting many immigrants to this country who will stay in rural parts for very long. Of course, that situation may change-I am seeking to avoid controversy as much as possible-as a result of the economic pause that the Minister of Trade and Commerce forecast at the end of the year. It may be that the situation will become quite different.
But in the days when I was responsible for the department, in the days when we were in office, when this country was going ahead and expanding and immigrants were coming here in large numbers they were attracted to the places where they could earn a living the fastest and in general those places were either in the cities or on the great construction projects. I should like to say here, and I am sure the minister will agree with me, that we could never have had the great growth and development and above all the immense construction there has been in this country in the past 12 years if we had not had these million immigrants who produced many of the people who did the hard, tough work that the older inhabitants of this country did not do and did not want to do because they had better jobs doing something else. I think those of us who have enjoyed the wonderful conditions we have had in this country in recent years, under that spirit of hope and optimism based on sound material development, should always remember that if it had not been for these newcomers who came to our country since the war and added to the greatest wealth we have of all, our human wealth, Canada would not be anything like the country it is today.


I am not going to criticize the minister for continuing the expedient which I adopted before the election of instructing the department to issue no visas for open placement of immigrants valid after the 31st of July. I should like to repeat what I said on October 17 about this matter. It was quite apparent to me by the very early spring that we were going to have an unprecedented influx of immigrants into Canada in the year 1957, and if the minister when he speaks is able to give us figures as to the total number, statistics on their distribution as between provinces, country of origin and other interesting information I am sure it would be of great interest to the committee. I think the minister is entitled to a little credit for this.
The minister pressed me very hard a couple of years ago, in the days when we were in office and referred estimates to committees where there was an opportunity to have a really detailed consideration of them, to attempt by expanding the scope of the assisted passage loans to encourage the increase of British immigration. I accepted the hon. gentleman's advice, rather sceptically, I admit. I did not see how the adoption of this policy could do any real harm and I thought it was worth trying to see whether it would do some good. I think it did. If the hon. member for Kamloops wants to take credit for that when he next appeals to his electors, he can make a note of it.
But whatever he may have done, whatever I may have done, whatever circumstances may have done, there is no question that in the year 1957 and, indeed, from about April, 1956, if my memory serves me right, there was a steady rise in the active interest in immigration to Canada from the United Kingdom. There was also a very encouraging kind of immigrant coming forward. As some hon. members who were here in the last parliament will recall, I had occasion at the end of November and beginning of December, after we had brought the session to a close so that hon. gentlemen opposite could have their convention without distraction by other duties, to go abroad because of the events in Hungary which created an unprecedented situation for which the hon. gentleman also had some share of responsibility. I took the occasion, while I was abroad to visit the United Kingdom at a time when we had
3,000	people going through the office in London in a single day, when the doors had to be closed about every hour because it was just unsafe to allow any more people in the building. I was very much encouraged about the future. It was surprising what a large proportion of these immigrants were young couples with one or two children. I talked to

a few of them, and I talked to the immigration officials who were dealing with them day by day in numbers which we have not seen since before the first world war.
The thing that was most interesting about this movement was the fact that most of these married couples said they did not really expect to be very much better off in Canada, but they were coming to Canada because they believed it would be a better country for their children and would give their children a better hope for the future. I feel we are making no mistake in encouraging people like that to come to Canada in just as large numbers as they can possibly be employed here.
As I started to say, when I digressed a little, I have no criticism to make of the minister for persisting in the device which I took before the election in order to gain time to see what the situation would be like at the end of June by stopping the granting of visas for open placement. There was a danger, as there is when big movements of this kind are under way, whether in investment or immigration or anything of that sort in a period of expansion, that it is going to go a little too far. There was a danger that a number of people would arrive in this country who could not find employment when they got here, and who would become disappointed, disgruntled and go back home. As a result of this a counter movement might tend to set in which would discourage healthy immigration in the future.
I say I have no criticism of the minister for having continued that policy. I was critical of the minister, and I am still critical of the minister for stopping rather abruptly and in a manner that was misunderstood- it was more a matter of bad public relations perhaps than bad policy-the movement of Hungarians. The minister will recall that he and I never quite agreed about this Hungarian movement. The minister said, and I will not take the trouble of putting the statement on the record now because I know there will be no dispute between us about it, that we should take Hungarian refugees absolutely without restriction. He said that at the time of the Hungarian uprising. The minister has never made any pretence that he did not say that at the time. I took the view that while we should do everything we could to encourage these people to come here we had to take some account of how many we could absorb, and that bringing Hungarian refugees here to live in camps was not really going to better their situation. Until they could be brought here with some reasonable hope of being established so that they could look forward to some sort of
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration future, I felt they would be better to be in camps in Europe. I felt we should try to hold out hope to them that we would take as many as we could, and that we would keep some of them coming all the time. I am very glad that the minister and his colleagues in the government, on further consideration, decided shortly after the opening of parliament to open the doors a little wider to help some of these unfortunate people to come here. I certainly commend the government for this, and have no criticism of it.
I do think we would all of us appreciate the minister's estimate of prospects for the year 1958, because of the almost unprecedented way in which we find ourselves dealing now with the 1957 estimates. Perhaps the minister will tell me that this is a very improper question and that I ought to wait until the next session of parliament. If the minister would give us a reasonable guarantee that the next session of parliament would be opening about the middle of February and that about the end of the month we would consider his estimates, I would be quite satisfied with that answer.
I want to say a word or two about what I regard as the most important of all the branches of the department, not perhaps in its impact on the Canadian economy but as a sacred trust to the Canadian people. I refer to the Indian affairs branch. It does seem to me, that the greatest responsibility we have as a civilized nation is to see that these people, the descendants of those people who possessed this country before we did, are as quickly as possible brought into a position where they have equal opportunities and equal advantages with other Canadians. I am not going to talk about the franchise except to make one statement. I was very unhappy, as minister, about the fact that the Indians do not have the franchise. I do believe that the sooner they have it the sooner we can be reasonably sure that their claims will commend wider support everywhere.
However, I admit there is a problem in connection with the franchise, and a very difficult problem. It is this. Under the Income Tax Act the Indians are given exemption from income tax on the income-
Order. I am sorry, but I have to advise the hon. member that his time has expired.

This department is divided into two sections, and this afternoon I want to deal with the second section. Since I first came to the House of Commons I have brought this problem before the house and before previous ministers, and I have stated on each occasion that I was not approaching this problem with any political

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration bias. I stated I was prepared to work in cooperation with any minister who headed this department. I must say that in the past my relations have been very good with these ministers, and I offer the same co-operation to the present minister. I have not been able to persuade them that some of the solutions I offered were good ones, but I think some little headway was made on the problem to which I am referring.
I refer to the shocking conditions under which about 2,000 people are living in my constituency and the area adjacent to it. They have been living under these conditions for many years. The problem is not one that can be solved overnight. It is going to take a lot of time and a lot of work. Perhaps for the information of new members I might outline the problem. It has to do with the living conditions of these people, the most of whom live in shacks made of logs with earthen roofs. I have pressed the government in the past to do something about housing conditions, and there has been little progress made. For instance, in the period from 1950 to 1956 there were 67 houses built. I pressed the previous minister very hard, especially two years ago, to get these people out of these shacks in which they were living.
They were unhealthy in the first place. Many of the shacks, which were not more than 14 feet, 16 feet or 18 feet square, had six to eight people living in them all winter long. The people could not even open a window. The only time they could get fresh air was when they brought in an armful of wood. I was disappointed that last year only five shacks were built on these reserves. I was given to understand that a considerable number were going to be built. When the minister is preparing his estimates for the coming year I hope that greater provision will be made for the building of houses on these Indian reserves.
These people have not much of a way to make a living. There have been some improvements. The previous government set up a loan fund whereby Indians could borrow money and start farming, buy a little bit of farm machinery and so on. That measure was not too successful. The main reason for that result was that adequate supervision was not given. There was a time not very many years ago when each Indian reserve had an instructor on it. The men that were hired were not of a good kind. A great many of them obtained the job- and I am going to say this-because they belonged to a political party. Many of them were old men who had been failures at everything else. They were not a good type of men. Good men were needed.


When that plan was first instituted these Indians did not know how to operate farm machinery. They did not even know how to take care of stock. Supervision was lacking. I do not know what changed the policy of the government but later they cut down on the number of what they called farm instructors. Today in my constituency in one case one man is looking after three reserves. Another man is looking after two reserves. In that particular case there are 90 miles between the two reserves. He cannot give proper supervision. One of the suggestions that I am going to make today is that the government see to it that they hire a good type of agriculturalist who knows how to farm and who would go on these reserves and help the Indians to farm properly.
As to some of these Indians who started farming five, six or seven years ago, conditions have not been too good and crops have not been too good. That is partly their own fault and partly because they were not properly supervised. Many of them have become discouraged. A few of them have been able to repay the loans but a great many of them have not been able to do so. The result is that today in many cases their machinery is worn out. Last summer when I made [DOT] a tour through the constituency I was amazed to find hundreds of acres gone back to weeds. I asked the Indians this question, "Why have you let this land go back to weeds?" They replied, "Our machinery is worn out; we have no horses; the department will not lend us any more money". Of course, I cannot blame the department too much for not lending any more money if the first loans were not repaid. But I believe they should have proper supervision, proper advice and proper leadership. That is why I stress the point that the men who are put in as instructors should know something, should have about them a little something that will encourage the Indians and lead them along, and should be men who will teach them to do these things properly.
We had a problem with regard to schools. That problem has been partly provided for because we now have an Indian school on each reserve. However the big problem there is to get qualified teachers. In many cases these schoolhouses are not well located in the reserves. Some of them are a long way back from the highway. It is extremely hard to get to them, especially when it rains or in winter when there is snow on the ground. It is extremely hard to get good teachers in the first place, and then it is difficult to get the teachers to stay after they have been obtained. I think that better provision should be made for roads where there is a school. Surely a road should be made so

that the schoolteacher can get out on the weekends at least to civilization. I think that decent teacherages should be built which would be more comfortable.
Another thing I suggest is that in most of these areas power is now available. It may be necessary for it to be brought in a few miles. I think that power should be provided to the schools on these particular reserves. I think a good look should be taken at the schools. Last summer I went out with the Catholic priest who looks after the reserves in the Battleford area, Father Paradis. One of the schools is set back quite a long way from the highway. It is not in a good location. If that school were moved even three or four miles to a new location it would be far easier for the Indians to get their children to the school. That particular school-and I am going to mention the name of it so that the minister can take note of it-is on the Sweet Grass reserve. The only provision for the teacher, who happens to be a married lady with two or three children, is three rooms in the end of the schoolhouse. I suggest that that schoolhouse be moved a couple of miles and a basement dug. I think it is important to have a basement in the school so that the children can go down there when the weather is bad. I suggest that a proper teacherage be built so that this worthy lady could be able to take care of her children in a decent home. They are crowded in three small rooms in that particular school. If the school were moved a couple of miles they would also have a place for a sports ground. I think it is necessary to encourage the young Indian children to go in for sports. They like to play football, and hockey and to take part in sports.
I want to go back for a moment to housing and make one suggestion. I understand from the officials of the department that the Thunderchild Indian reserve own a timber tract somewhere to the north of their reserve. I am suggesting to the government that the department take a look at this timber tract in order to see whether or not there is building timber there. As to the reserve of Red Pheasant, the Indians there tell me that there are thousands of good poplar logs which would make lumber. I think it would be a splendid idea if, after this matter is looked into, it could be decided that it is practical to put in a small sawmill, thus giving some of the Indians some work in sawing some of these logs up into lumber, not only to help provide work for the Indians but to provide them with material with which to build houses.

I took a good look at some of these reserves last year and in many cases there is a wonderful potential if the reserves were properly developed. I am taking as examples two reserves in particular, namely the Mosquito Stoney reserve and the Red Pheasant reserve. They are situated about 35 miles south of the town of Battleford. The Mosquito reserve has a total acreage of 31,540 acres. However, it is estimated by the departmental officials, as given in an answer to a question I had on the order paper last year, that 12,624 acres of that reserve are arable. I might say here that that is not first-class wheat land but it is good land for oats, barley or feed.
The Red Pheasant reserve has an acreage of 24,320 acres of which 8,502 acres are arable. The two reserves are side by side and they have together 21,126 acres of arable land. The population on these reserves is about, 370 people.
I know two ministers who are greatly interested in some kind of development scheme and I am speaking now of religious ministers and not ministers in the house. Their names are Father Paradis and Canon Wickenden. I believe these two men are dedicated men. They belong to different churches and they both took the trouble to learn to speak the Cree language so that they might get close to these people. They are vitally interested in seeing something done towards developing these reserves and making it possible to bring up the living standards of these people without a great cost to the people of Canada.
I would suggest to the minister that he go outside of his own department to the Department of Agriculture and either put the scheme I am going to outline up to that department to develop or else get the proper kind of men to run it. I believe that if such a development scheme was put into operation those reserves would carry at least 2,000 head of cattle. They would not carry them all at once, of course, but I suggest this should be done in stages. The first stage would be for the department to go into the whole project with the Indian bands themselves and come to some kind of agreement whereby the Indians would agree to turn over control of the project to the department for a term of years, say 15, 20 or 25 years or whatever the agricultural experts might figure would be the proper length of time.
Next, parliament should supply the necessary funds. Thirdly, I have already stated that the control of the program should be under the Department of Agriculture. Fourthly, the object of the program would be first to provide work and wages to as many Indians as possible and to get them away from the terrible relief system which we have had in the past

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration few years. Last year there was almost $100,000 supplied in relief by the Battleford agency and I think that is a disgrace. What could we have done with a development program if we had had $100,000? It would provide, after the scheme got into working order, for the training of young people in methods of farming and would take care of the needy on the reserves, thus eliminating the necessity for this government to supply a huge amount of money for relief of those people over the years.
Fifthly, I believe that such a scheme as this, properly worked out and properly supervised, could repay every cent advanced by the government. I believe repayments should be made in annual installments starting about five years after commencement of the operation. Any balance left over from those payments could go to the band fund to care for needy people on the reserves and at the conclusion of the contract the project should be turned over to the Indians at such time as they could prove to be responsible. It might, of course, take some time to train the right kind of Indians to assume responsibility for a project of this kind.
I have outlined a scheme which I have talked over at great length with both of the gentlemen I have mentioned. We spent many hours together working out a rough idea of what should be done and I believe an immediate start should be made. For instance our Indians are always short of work in the wintertime and many of them could be put to work this winter getting out pickets. One of the first things to do would be to fence this whole reserve and next spring we could have some of them digging up stones. As soon as the project could be decided upon the proper machinery could be purchased and the necessary buildings put up.
I think a scheme should be devised whereby a village or townsite should be set up and instead of having shacks scattered four, five, or six miles apart all over the reserve, which makes it hard for the Indians to get their children to school, the idea of building up a village should be envisaged. Bring in power; bring in some of the amenities which we white people have in Canada.
As I have said before, I think we should be prepared to go into cattle as soon as possible. I would not suggest that many cattle be bought to start with. Hay could be put in next summer and cattle purchased to the extent of whatever feed is available. Another thing I think should be done next summer is the development of a good gardening patch. I am sure most people in this house would be astonished to find that these people do not


grow garden vegetables, with very few exceptions although there are exceptions. I went into an Indian's home last year and he took me down into his basement. He had vegetables and his wife had canned stuff but he was the only Indian of whom I know in my constituency who milks a few cows. There is no need for Indians to live on the kind of rations upon which they do live. I have a list of them here but I do not have time to go into them now. I think we should set about preparing and growing garden patches as soon as possible as this is essential.
I spoke a little earlier about the wrong type of men being put on these reserves as instructors. The department of Indian affairs had a good instructor by the name of Jimmy Warden and some of the officials will remember his name. His father was a North West Mounted Policeman and this boy was raised on the reserve and learned to speak Cree. He grew up with the Indians and when his father died he was put in as a farm instructor. That is the kind of man who is needed. He liked the Indians and they liked him and he had them growing vegetables in large quantities. They had 300 head of cattle on the reserve at that time, which was 25 or 30 years ago, while today there are 100 head of cattle on the reserve and they are not growing any vegetables at all.
I saw a potato patch at one Indian home last summer. They had it up on a gravel knoll. It would not grow potatoes in any circumstances. They had it in the wrong place. I think it is possible that this sort of thing could be rectified, given a little common sense and a little planning. The whole situation as it exists today is deplorable, and we in this country should not stand for it. There are 2,000 people in my constituency living under these conditions. We should not allow them to go on and on in this way and I hope the minister will co-operate with them and look into this problem. I suggest we start with one reserve and try it out, and then, if the scheme works, introduce it into other reserves.

Mr. Chairman, in dealing with the estimates of this department we know we will be called upon to approve an expenditure, much of which has already been spent, of approximately $41 million.
This makes this department of great importance financially, but in the way in which it affects our economy and way of life it is a very important department as well. It is under the leadership at the present time of a very able minister, though, I am sorry to say, he is just an acting minister. I believe this department is worthy of a full time minister. However, I have no criticism to make

of the present leadership. As I say, the acting minister is an able administrator; he is assisted by an active parliamentarian and I am satisfied he is backed up by a very efficient staff. In my personal dealings with this department I have always been given a very cordial hearing, my complaints have been adjusted to my entire satisfaction, and I am going to say that the relationship so far as I am concerned is very acceptable.
While I am in this happy frame of mind I should like also to commend the department for a couple of things which they have done during the past few months. First, I have noticed that there is a more humane approach to the problem of allowing immediate members of Chinese and Asiatic families to come to Canada where they may be reunited with their husbands, fathers or children who may have been allowed entry into this country in past years, I am also going to commend the department for having taken a second look at our immigration requirements, and for slowing down the flow to allow a careful study to be made of Canada's need for more people, and a careful study of the type of people still needed to man our economy.
Mr. Chairman, I say "still needed" for I feel that Canada's greatest need is a very largely increased population, and our efforts must continue to that end. However, at a time like this when a recession in business is causing concern among our working men and women it would be folly to continue the flow of those who would be dependent on employment and who would enter into competition with our native labour force. It therefore showed good judgment when the department saw fit to take action to slow down the flow of people entering this country. The conditions through which we are now passing are ample proof that our policy must be very flexible in order to meet just such a situation as we face at the present time. Careful planning is needed at all times in order to evaluate our requirements and to designate the type and class of workers needed so that only those who would fit into our labour force and who would not disrupt our economy are brought in. I think this is something which should at no time be lost sight of.
In addition, our immigration policy must be selective. The right to enter Canada should not be too lightly bestowed. Of course, the ideal immigrant would be a worker bringing with him possibly three or four dependants. Those dependants would become consumers of goods in this country and we would not have an improper balance as between labour and consumers. Then, of course, there are professional men or
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration women and technicians who may want to come to Canada. I do not think anyone will dispute that at the present time we need doctors, dentists, engineers of all kinds, chemists and technicians and I would strongly recommend to the department that it should make every effort to promote the interest of these classes of people when they come to.Canada, and encourage them to every extent possible. Bringing them to Canada is not all that must be done.
We are continually reading of cases where professional men, especially doctors and dentists, are finding it difficult to become established in practice in Canada. This is not the fault of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, but it arises through what might be called the closed compact of professional organizations among doctors and dentists which is making it difficult for these people to comply with regulations before beginning to practice in this country. I consider that at a time like this when these people are so urgently needed the department should consider taking some action which might help to ease the present situation, and investigate complaints brought to its attention.
Mr. Chairman, there are other factors to be considered in selecting immigrants besides their status in the economy on their arrival. Consideration must be given to their religion and to their political background at all times. We believe that all men are born equal regardless of race or creed. But we also believe that our immigration department must be careful to regulate admissions so as not to upset the balance of our social life. We know that due to immigration we will become an increasingly cosmopolitan nation. But let us see that Canadians of tomorrow will be Canadians who will possess the same physical attributes and continue to foster the same ideas as those which we of this generation are trying to develop, namely the ideals of tolerance and freedom. I do not think any department can exercise greater influence on the future of Canada than can the Department of Citizenship and Immigration by building up our population to a level which can make full use of our great natural resources and industrial capacity. I would emphasize that the slogan must be carefully selected.
May I say just a word about citizenship? The right to live in a country entails certain responsibilities, the chief of which is service to the country in which one is living. I once heard the governor of one of the greatest service clubs make a statement in speaking of service and I know I shall never forget it. He said that service is the rent

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration which we pay for the right to live in our country or our community. I think that is something that every Canadian could well take to heart. It should be impressed upon those who are thinking of coming to Canada and who have an idea of becoming Canadian citizens; but in order to give that full measure of service as residents of any country, I believe a person must be a citizen of that country.
Since I have said that-and I believe it- I am going to suggest that the department study the question of compulsory citizenship. Some policy should be formulated toward this end. Possibly it could be done by a person who has recently come to this country being compelled to sign a declaration of intent that he is going to become a Canadian citizen, after a specified time, maybe one year or two years. After he has done this it should be possible for him, in co-operation with the department, to study the obligations and the rights of citizenship and after a reasonable period apply for the right to become a Canadian citizen. I say "right" Mr. Chairman; I would like to say privilege for I do honestly believe it is a privilege to be a Canadian citizen.
I am now going to say just a few words about Indian affairs. I have spoken on this in past years. I think the committee is well aware of my stand. I was keenly interested in, and I fully endorse, the speech of the hon. member for The Battlefords who has just taken his seat. Much can be done to improve the lot of the Indian and I am going to close with this. The program should be one committed to removing the Indian from his position as a ward of the government and to making him a first-class Canadian citizen who may be assimilated into the Canadian way of life.

Mr. Chairman, I have some rather unpleasant things to say this afternoon for a few minutes, and I shall say them entirely on my own responsibility as a member of parliament and at the request of certain members of the seafarers' international union who visited my office, certain members of various unions affiliated with the Canadian Labour Congress and certain other seamen whom I met either in my office, in my home or in Vancouver.
Before I proceed I might say that my mother was in the habit of saying that when you have an important matter of principle to deal with consider it well. When you are convinced you are right you should then fix bayonets and charge. That is what I am going to do this afternoon. I received my information from conversations I have had with a good number of people whose

integrity I have no question about, from correspondence and from research conducted by others very interested in the development of the labour movement in Canada and progressive social legislation in Canada. In fact, in one or two cases where the information had been a bit startling I inquired as to the person in question and was informed on the authority of very substantial citizens interested in the labour movement and, in some cases, interested in our policies that these people were sound persons and I could rely upon the information they had given me.
My subject, this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, is the responsibility of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration for the continued domicile in Canada of one known as Harold Chamberlain Banks, particularly in view of the representations made in this house by some present members of the government with respect to the admissibility of this person to Canada who, we discovered at that time, has a criminal record in the United States but who has been able to remain in Canada by not completing a complete immigration application.
In developing my case to indicate the attitude of the members of the government in this respect I wish to quote from Hansard of July 21, 1955, where the present Postmaster General had this to say, as reported at page 6537:
As I have said, unions as such have contributed tremendously to our Canadian economy. We respect them. We admire them. We need them. But a union or any group in the hands of the wrong people can be turned to devious ends.
What is Banks? I have previously referred to him as a labour racketeer. I now refer to him in some detail as a man who has been convicted of certain crimes in Canada; a man who has had certain convictions-one of them carrying 14 years -in the United States; a man who, among other things, has been charged-although I do net suggest he was convicted-with the possession of firearms, murder and child-stealing. Incidentally it is rather amusing that in the article which sets out these various aspects of Mr. Banks, the writer says this;
"When I mentioned this generally to Mr. Banks, he said something to the effect that most of it stemmed from his long labours on behalf of trade unionism."
During that debate, or in a previous debate, I am not sure which, the present Secretary of State expressed her views on this matter very strongly indeed. I have also had occasion to express my views as a result of meeting some of these men. I said at that time, as reported at page 6538 of Hansard:
Quite a number of good labour people, men who have worked all their lives in the labour movement, are concerned about the damage this character is doing to the good name of labour in Canada.
Then I finished up by giving my information respecting the accumulation of property

on the part of this person who, I am informed, came into Canada about 1954. Later in my remarks I said, as reported at page 6539 of Hansard:
I shall conclude by suggesting there should be an investigation by the Department of Labour, and by the Department of National Revenue as to the personal funds that Mr. Banks accumulates, in order to protect our seamen, the best interests of this country and the good name of organized labour.
Now, Mr. Chairman, after committing a crime in Canada which was the smuggling of cigarettes, at which time his Cadillac was seized

I understand he has two Cadillacs; not many of us in this house drive Cadillacs -but later his Cadillac was returned, he was fined $200 and he was allowed to remain in Canada as a landed immigrant as a result of an order in council recommended by the previous minister of finance, Mr. Harris, to the cabinet. I think this is the first instance of a showing of lack of courage in dealing with a situation such as this.
I have talked this over with members of the union and other seamen who say that he was brought here at the suggestion of the shipowners-I place a lot of responsibility on their shoulders for the situation in Canada today-in order to fight communist influence in the seamen's union of that day. There may be some validity in that statement, but I am also told by these very responsible seamen, thoroughly good characters-I may say I have gone to great pains to establish their background-that this is largely a myth, that the rank and file themselves had largely disposed of any communist influence before he arrived. I am a great believer in the rank and file if they have an opportunity to give effect to their opinions under the normal labour movement procedures of our country.
Let us have a look at his record. His record in the United States, or some parts of it, is well known. It has been placed on the records of the house by various members on several occasions. It has been the subject of articles in prominent magazines, periodicals and newspapers. I have had conversations with men who have told me that they have witnessed Mr. Harold Banks pulling a gun on a seaman in his office and having him beaten unmercifully by another colleague of his with a short piece of rubber hose.
When I was travelling west at the end of the 1956 session I had occasion to talk to three of the porters on the train, The Canadian, who at one time were stewards on ships in the Canada-West Indies service of Canadian National Steamships. They told me that they left their jobs with the steamship line running to the West Indies because
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of Mr. Harold Banks' dislike for negroes. These three men were born in Montreal and are Canadian citizens. I have had visits from other seamen who have told me of the complete lack of an understanding of democracy so far as Mr. Banks is concerned.
I understand that he is not now an official of the union-and I am not blaming the officials-but is now known as an adviser to the union.
Then I come to some evidence that shows that Mr. Banks appears to have done very well indeed. As the result of information brought to us by various seamen, some of us were interested in his acquisition of property and had a very careful search made in certain land registry offices for property acquired by Mr. Banks. I am going to give two illustrations. I had a search made in the land registry office in Vancouver and this is what I found. The person who writes me says:
I obtained the legal description of the property from the city hall and searched the records at the land registry office at the court house. Below is the information on record there. There have been no judgments against the property.
This is the transfer of the property from the union to Mr. Banks personally.

I come now to indicate the type of person who was allowed into Canada by this special order in council when the relatives of good Canadian citizens, because of some slight health defect, are denied admission to Canada; when also relatives of some good Chinese citizens, long-time residents who have lived in the country for 50 years or more are denied admission to Canada because of age and so on. Yet Mr. Banks is admitted by a special order in council. Those responsible ought to be ashamed of themselves.
I cannot go into this matter in full but I have here a copy of the Canadian Sailor published in Montreal under date of Wednesday, May 16, 1957. The leading editorial clearly indicates Mr. Banks' sympathies with regard to labour matters. It deals with the Beck-Hoffa trials in the United States and refers in effect to Beck's election as a triumph of democracy. The whole editorial shows that Mr. Banks believes in and supports this sort of thing. He is gloating over the fact that difficulty is being experienced in pinning down these two birds. Do we want that sort of thing in Canada? Mind you, I bring up these matters at the request of members of the union concerned, as I said before, and members of other unions who have no other place except the House of Commons in which to have this matter aired for the information of the public. I do so at their request as a representative of the people.
I notice that in the United States the official labour organizations have dealt pretty promptly with Beck and Hoffa. I also understand that at one time Mr. Banks was a close colleague of some of the men working in the longshoremen's union in New York, that element which does not believe in democracy. Yet Mr. Banks was accepted as a landed immigrant and is now applying for Canadian citizenship. I was very interested in his application as were a lot of other people in Canada. The number of rank and file members in the labour movement who are interested in this question is surprising. I wrote the clerk of the citizenship court in Montreal and asked for a copy of the stenographic 

report of the evidence which I was quite willing to pay for. I did not mind going without a meal or two in order to get it. Anyway, I received this reply:

I was then reduced to getting hold of the newspapers and I got some photostatic copies of the newspaper articles following the day of Mr. Banks' application for citizenship before this court. I am told by persons who were present that this is a fair report of what happened in the citizenship court. The article is headed, "Labour Chiefs Back Banks' Citizenship". It appeared in the Montreal Gazette of August 17, 1957. The sub-heading reads: "Police Captain also Praises Applicant." The article reads:
Hal C. Banks, international vice-president and Canadian "adviser" of the seafarers' international union received unqualified recommendations for Canadian citizenship yesterday from four top name labour leaders and a city police captain.
Judge Paul Fontaine sitting in citizenship court set next Friday for final pleas by lawyers in the case and will then forward his recommendations to Ottawa.
The tall Minnesota-born Banks was painted at last week's session of the court as an undesirable candidate for citizenship, with criminal convictions both in the U.S. and here. Opposition to the application, which may be made by "anyone", was presented to the judge by representatives of other unions and by seamen who claimed they had lost their livelihood as a result of Banks' methods of operating the S.I.U.
These objections were repeated and expanded yesterday and at the opening of the session a certified true copy of a local conviction was filed-*
Then, farther down we find this:
Claude Jodoin, president of the Canadian Labor Congress, with 1,123,000 members, and Frank Hall, president of the 500,000-member non-operating railway workers' union, were two of the witnesses heard yesterday who gave high praise to Banks as a good union administrator and worthy prospect for Canadian citizenship.
Then, later:
Mr. Hall told the court that it was at his suggestion that the S.I.U. sent one of its vicepresidents to Montreal in 1948 "because the S.I.U. here was in the hands of communists". It was at that time, said the witness, that he met the applicant.
That is Mr. Banks.
"I have always had a high opinion of his professional ability and capacity since," he said.
In recommending him as "a fit subject for Canadian citizenship," Mr. Hall said that he was speaking on behalf of his union.
"He has done something for Canada by cleaning up the communists in the union and by running a good organization,"-

Then Mr. Banks himself was a witness and the article says:
Banks himself was a witness yesterday and under examination by his counsel, John Ahern, Q.C., denied an opposing witness' statement that he had once stated he "could get rid of anyone in Montreal for ¥1,500." He thought he might have said that $1,500 severance pay would get rid of some inefficient union officials.
Then, I should like to quote from the Gazette of August 20, 1957, a column by Arthur Blakely. He has this to say:
He has been described as a labour "dictator". He has never, as far as is known, been elected to any office by the Canadian seamen whom he rules with an iron hand. During the first five years in which he headed his union, he didn't stand for election to any office. The constitution, as it then stood, didn't contain any provision for electing a president or director. And there didn't seem to be too much enthusiasm for the elective principle anyway.
A liberalized constitution adopted in 1954, to meet growing criticism, looked much better. But Mr. Banks emerged on the same old ruggedly individualistic non-elective basis as "adviser" to the union. And carried on, apparently, as before under his new title.
Even under the more generous constitution of 1954, elections may, it is reported, be participated in only by the union's "book" members. This excludes an estimated 80 per cent of the membership. And voting book memberships are distributed parsimoniously and on a highly selective basis.
Under Mr. Banks' guiding hand, the union makes extensive use of the Do Not Ship (DNS) list.
I never saw such an atmosphere of fear. I am not allowed to use the names of any of the men. They are afraid either of losing their jobs, being put on the do not ship list, or they say they are family men and they do not want anything to happen to them.
Any seaman whose name goes on the list finds it next to impossible to get employment. Mr. Banks has been accused of making extensive use of the DNS list as a handy means of disposing of personal enemies and union members who complain too noisily about alleged undemocratic practices within the union. Banks himself insists that the DNS list is used only to deal with communists, perverts and the like.
Other labor charges that have been levelled at Mr. Banks' leadership are that adequate union financial statements haven't been generally avail-akle>
that regular meetings aren't encouraged and that union officials have been deposed without cause. Through his high-wage policy, Mr. Banks is also accused of scuppering Canada's deep sea fleet by driving ships into foreign registry.
Now, I just want to mention an article in Canadian Labour of November, 1957. It is an excellent article and was written by Donald MacDonald, Canadian Labour Congress secretary. It is entitled Racketeering in the Labour Movement. I heartily agree with what he has to say in this article, and it shows the position of the labour movement in Canada on this sort of thing. It reads:
It is significant that the CLC has not found it necessary to set up an ethical practices committee similar to the one established by the AFL-CIO.

It is very obvious, after my reading of these press reports, that the gentlemen who appeared in support of Banks application were completely unaware of the facts surrounding this case, and this man's attitude towards the rank and file as well as the attitude of a good many of the rank and file towards him. So far as I can understand, the rank and file do not have any opportunity to express themselves. I have said, why don't you fellows go to the meetings; why don't you do something? They say it is hopeless because of the nature of the organization and their attitude towards being placed on this do not ship list.
In any event, the article goes on:
It Is well to remember. In any discussion of union racketeering, that there is a natural partner whose role is all too often ignored or toned down: the employer. It takes two to make an agreement, and, if a union officer wants to make a deal with an employer, there must be an employer willing to make a deal.
Then, he goes on:
In unionism, as in health, prevention is better than cure. Unfortunately, both seem to be required. The question is then a double one: how to prevent racketeering and how to stop it once it appears. So far as prevention is concerned, there are at least two solutions that come to mind. One is almost a cliche, but an irrefutable truth, none the less. A live, active membership, well-informed about the labour movement, ready to act in defence of a clean organization, is probably the best guarantee against racketeering that anyone could devise. Complementary to that, of course, and probably inevitable in such circumstances, is a leadership whose integrity is beyond question. To that might be added the willingness and ability to engage as union staff, people who have professional competence in insurance matters, or to use consultants of good reputation.
Now, Mr. Chairman, our labour movement in Canada has a splendid record and a democratic background. The type of life led by this man and his activities do not appeal to the men and women in our labour movement. In the early days of union organization in Great Britain, the movement attracted people largely because of their Christian beliefs. The history of the Canadian labour movement has been free of the sort of thing I have described, and that is something of which the labour movement can be proud.
I know this is a somewhat delicate subject, and I do not like doing this sort of thing. However, I feel it is the responsibility of someone to speak on this subject. I feel that there has been a lack of courage on the part of the former government, and to date I am of the opinion that there has been some lack of courage on the part of the present government. In fact, there has been a lack of courage in a good many people who should be concerned about this important matter.

I thank the members of the committee because I have only four or five brief recommendations to make. We are all concerned about the Canadian National shipping situation, about the men who are unemployed and the difficulties that have arisen. In the first instance I suggest, therefore, we could do something about it as members of parliament. We should use a little courage and the government should investigate the character of this man very fully, and then I am certain it would be well justified in deporting him as an undesirable person. Secondly, I would suggest to Canadian National Railways that they return these ships to Canadian registry, and that the company should make every effort to meet the elected officials of the union and re-open negotiations with a view to getting these ships operating again at the first opportunity.
I suggest that the government itself should take a lead in doing all that is possible to bring this unfortunate incident in Canadian labour relations to a satisfactory conclusion so that the ships will soon be operating, the men working again and our trade can be continued with the West Indies. Finally I suggest that the senior officials of the congress should use their good offices to do all that is possible to assist the local elected officers of the union with their negotiations and with their efforts to build a seafarers' international union that will be in line with labour traditions in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wonder whether I might just say a word on this particular subject. I will not attempt to answer the general remarks that have been made-I expect there are still others who wish to speak-but in view of
[Mr. Herridge.)

what has just been said by the hon. member for Kootenay West I think I should say a word now about the Banks situation.
First, 1 should like to express, I am sure, on behalf of the members of the house appreciation to the hon. gentleman for having decided to bring the matter forward. It is an important matter. It is not an easy matter to deal with judicially or with the absence of partiality. The hon. gentleman has done so with a commendable degree of success. He has stated the facts, he has left no doubt as to his own attitude in the matter, but he has not indulged in exaggeration or vicious or unnecessary criticism.
However, the government is in this position. Without for a moment accepting either the hon. member's suggestion that there is a lack of courage on our part and without accepting any suggestion that may be made that we are trying to find a reason for deferring action, I as minister am obliged to say that not only can we not act at this moment but that it is extremely difficult for us to say anything for the reason that Mr. Banks' application is now before the citizenship court in Montreal and will, quite possibly, come before me for decision.
The situation is that if the court rejects the application, then I believe that I have no further role to perform in the citizenship matter. If, however, the court should accept and approve the application then it will be referred to the minister for confirmation or rejection. I am therefore in the position where this case may come before me any day now, and I think it would be highly improper for me at this point to express any attitude which would amount in effect to prejudging the case.
In the same way, however, I might attempt to divorce the immigration side of it from the citizenship side and to deal with the charge made by the hon. member that there was something improper about his previous admission and the order in council which provided that he should be granted the status of landed immigrant, I do not think personally that I could do that and discuss that matter-approve or condemn or criticize, whatever I might do-without clearly indicating my attitude towards the whole subject. Again, therefore, I think the only position I can take is to say that I am inhibited from discussing this matter until I have reached a decision and have announced that decision on the citizenship case when and if that case comes before me.
I may say this, however. I will undertake, if the house is in session-or if the house is not in session, as soon as it meets again and

if I should still be responsible for this department-to go into all proper details with regard to any decision we may have arrived at and with regard to our attitude on the whole question. I want to assure the hon. gentleman and the committee that I think they will find that we do not lack courage either in the facing up to the decision that we have to make, whatever it may be, or in the discussing of the matter when I feel that we are in a position to do so.
I would only say this in addition with regard to what the hon. member for Kootenay West has said. While I appreciate to the full the difficult position in which his informants have been placed, it is quite impossible for any responsible government or responsible minister to act upon the basis of such information. The Immigration Act and the Canadian Citizenship Act lay down the things which are required to be established before certain decisions can be taken and certain courses can be followed. It is proof, facts, verdicts of courts and such things as that which are required. No decisive action could ever be taken on the basis of statements as to which the person making the statements says, "I am not in a position to go to court if necessary and repeat my statements under oath in court"-or even to let his name be used. I therefore hope that those who have given information one way or the other to the hon. gentleman and to others will in order to help us clear up this whole matter, eventually bring themselves to the position where they can say, "We are prepared not only to give this information privately but to give it in court if necessary".

I should like to say just a word on this matter. I agree completely with everything the minister has said. I would hope that no member of the committee would seek to press this matter and to prejudge the issue. On a good many occasions I have been in the position in which the minister now finds himself, and I made the resolve that if I was ever in a different position, knowing as I do how difficult it is to exercise the quasi judicial functions that parliament imposes upon the minister of this department, I would never press-and that I would urge my friends not to do so-the minister into making premature or prejudicial observations about a matter about which he must make a judgment on a set of facts all of which are not before him at the time. I would hope that the hon. member for Kootenay West would not press the matter at the present time. It seems to me that the attitude of the minister is the only proper and civilized one in all the circumstances.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the subject of citizenship and immigration. May I at the outset congratulate the acting minister on the honour bestowed upon him by his government in appointing him to this important office.
Being one of those who are very much interested in the program of citizenship and immigration, I welcome this occasion as one affording an opportunity to pay tribute to the wise and courageous policy of immigration of the Liberal administrations of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mackenzie King. In particular, it is owing to the faithful and diligent application of the liberal policies of immigra-ton by Mr. Harris and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that Canada has been served so well and has achieved such an enviable record. I regret, however, that the Tory governments have never had a positive policy, or I should say, even the slightest semblance of a policy of immigration for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What nonsense.

Unfortunately they have
rather discouraged the growth and development of Canada by their unrealistic conservative attitude to the problem of immigration.
The present administration, in one of its first public announcements upon having assumed office, on July 1, 1957 restricted immigration from Europe. That action virtually shut the door to a flow into Canada of people yearning to regain freedom and to flee from communist persecution.
Canadians who still have relatives and friends suffering in these countries behind the iron curtain, in Austria and in Italy, are desirous of extending all help and merciful treatment to these their relatives. I should say that these Canadians are not only disappointed but in many cases are outraged by the restrictive and unjust attitude of the Conservative government's immigration program.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman was in the committee when the former minister spoke. If he was, I wonder whether he agreed with what was said when
