Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the former minister indicated that he had made the same decision himself with regard to the Hungarians and that he was in agreement with our confirming it.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman, since he presumes to interpret what I said, will not mind my making a comment here. I said I had no quarrel with the attitude which the government had taken to open placement immigrants and open placement immigrants are not the relatives of Canadians who happen to be refugees. I did dissent from what the minister had done about refugees.

I also wish to draw to the attention of this committee the stand taken by the present government when it was fighting the election before June 10. We heard many brave and outspoken promises of the present Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and of the leader of the present government with respect to increased immigration. What do we see now? They have a policy which they treat as though they were turning a tap on and off, willy nilly.
The figure of 22 million predicted by the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects as the forecast of population for the year 1970 can hardly be expected to be reached if the present restrictive measures are pursued by this government. It was the firm conclusion of that royal commission that the growth of Canada's population is the principal factor in the economic development and prosperity of this country and we all know very well that Canada always experienced tremendous and unparalled economic development, prosperity and population increase during the Liberal administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mackenzie King and Louis St. Laurent, all of whom gave Canada a realistic and therefore a successful immigration policy.
I am proud to be a descendant of a Polish immigrant who settled in this fortunate and pleasant country during the progressive immigration program of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the year 1910. Ever since that time Liberal governments have fostered an increase in Canada's population by admitting people from continental Europe whose industriousness and whose cherished possessions of great traditions and cultures 1,000 years old or more and whose first-hand experiences in the fight against communist exploitation and persecution have already immeasurably contributed and will continue to contribute to the stature of this great country.
This enviable mosaic composed of different sizes, shapes and colours is, may I assure you Mr. Chairman, cemented not only by a


common allegiance to the crown and a common Canadian citizenship but also by strong conviction of loyalty, pride and faith in the past, present and future of Canada.
Sir Casimir Gzowski, the first Polish settler in Toronto, contributed so much in the building of bridges, roads and railways in Ontario that he merited the distinction of being honoured by a knighthood by Queen Victoria. The hundreds and thousands of immigrants who followed him have already served Canada well with brain and brawn and in the armed forces they, with their sons, have on many occasions distinguished themselves. I want only to mention at this time Pilot Officer Andrew Myrarski from Winnipeg who was the first R.C.A.F. member to be awarded the Victoria Cross.
These are some of the reasons why I am proud to belong to that party which has always been foremost in fostering the pride of our people in a common citizenship in which all Canadians are treated as equals regardless of race, colour or creed. Canada can be proud of the fact that the Liberal ministers of immigration initiated and expanded an active program of promoting Canadian citizenship among newly arrived immigrants.
While speaking on this subject I would like to congratulate the Liberal administration for its attitude towards the administration of Canadian Indian affairs. I wish also to pay tribute to those valiant Canadian women in the Order of the Grey Nuns and also to the missionaries who have contributed so much to making better Canadians of the Indian people.
Turning now to certain specific problems I would like to ask the Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration whether his government has any policy for prospective immigrants from the British West Indies which area is now in the British commonwealth of nations. Many of these West Indians live in my constituency and they would like to have their relatives join them in Canada. Furthermore I have received several petitions from Canadians in my constituency who have distant blood relatives such as nephews and cousins behind the iron curtain. The situation which now exists in these communist countries is well known to all hon. members but the very restrictive policy of the present administration is preventing these people from entering Canada and thereby escaping from communist persecution.
Other petitions have come to me from people who have very close relatives in the state of Israel. On grounds of compassion they have asked for the admission to Canada of such relatives as their own brothers and

sisters or their sole living relatives and I am sorry to say that these petitions, one after another, have been turned down by the present administration.
There is another problem which I would like to draw to the attention of the acting minister and that is with respect to petitions which have been forwarded to me by Polish people in Canada for admission to this country of several hundreds of Poles from displaced persons camps in Austria in addition to several thousands of Croatians who also wish to come to Canada and have been unsuccessful in doing so. I would ask the minister to have his department investigate these matters.
Lastly I would like the minister to look into cases where persons who have spent a few weeks or a month in psychiatric hospitals either for observation or treatment of minor ills or for nervous breakdowns have been refused applications for Canadian citizenship.

Mr. Chairman, the acting minister has had many tributes from all sections of the house and I share these views. I feel he will have been somewhat embarrassed to have a former minister of citizenship and immigration speak of him in the way he did.
The minister did get his Department of Justice estimates through very quickly a week ago but I do not believe he will be able to dispose of these estimates quite so quickly. I realize that with three quarters of a million people in Canada seeking employment at the moment it is not very popular to advocate additional immigration but I do feel the sixteen million people living in the northern part of this continent, cannot expect to hold these rich lands exclusively for ourselves.
I am sure there is no one here who will dispute my claim that 30 million people might well enjoy a higher standard of living than we have here in Canada today. I realize we are not doing any good service by asking people to come here and share employment with us. I think we must do two things; we must see that the standard of living for the people of Canada is increased, and we must see that more people are permitted to come here. I know there is a regulation which will permit 50 people to come to Canada from Ceylon in addition to those who normally come to this country. I may advise the committee that I have recently been to Ceylon, and although Ceylon is less than half as large as the Mackenzie constituency, eight million people live in that country as compared with our 45,000, and I say without boasting that nowhere in Asia did I see such fine fertile
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration land as we have in north Saskatchewan. I do not think the people of Canada should expect that we should limit the people coming to this country to such small numbers.
I should like the minister, when he has an opportunity, to bring us up to date regarding the argument advanced by his colleague the Minister of Public Works on August 8, 1956 in connection with the regulations affecting immigration from India. The Minister of Public Works said on that occasion:
I should like to also urge upon the minister that he reconsider the provisions with regard to immigration from India. One significant fact is that India is a sister nation of the commonwealth and I think that should be borne in mind at all times.
The minister will recall that members from this party and from his own party made very effective representations to the department regarding this situation. speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My recollection is that the question asked was whether there had been any change in procedure. I did not regard this as procedure. This was not regarded as being covered by the terms of the hon. gentleman's question. I thought what the


hon. gentleman had in mind was something that would require an order in council, something that would require a firm administrative directive applicable at all levels. It seemed to me that the question of whether the minister or head office reviewed the Chinese file could hardly be described as being within the ambit of the question. I am very glad to have the matter cleared up, however, and I have no desire to get into a quarrel about semantics with the minister. I am not saying the answer was misleading, but it did mislead me.

1.	Has any change been made in the procedure for dealing with Chinese immigration applications since June 21, 1957?

And so on. I may say that reading this in context I think the committee will agree that we were justified in the department in concluding that this question was asking: when you have received an application for admission, have you changed the procedure for dealing with it. We certainly answered it in that sense not realizing that the hon. gentleman's question was: have you changed the policy for reviewing the applications which may have been on file for many years.

I assure the committee that I was not suggesting for one moment there was any bad faith in the answer I received, though there does seem to be some difference about the interpretation of the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
And as many times as a review is requested?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have not found it necessary yet to consider any limitation on the number of times we review the cases.
You have not answered my last question.
On request, would the minister review decisions made since June 21?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes.
Progress reported.

Can the hon. gentleman who is leading the house indicate what the business will be on Friday and Saturday?
Business of the House

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My Speaker, you will recall it was agreed that the house would rise at six o'clock today and would then stand adjourned until eleven o'clock on Friday morning. On Friday it is proposed to take Bill No. 237, to provide for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural products, and after that to proceed in committee of supply with the estimates of citizenship and immigration.
Will that be the program also on Saturday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot make any positive
statement at this moment as regards the program for Saturday.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to the special order of the house passed on January 11, 1958.
